about: This is the complete TIH Entrepreneurship & Startup Launch Program, rebuilt into twenty modules that take you from mindset and idea all the way to a launched, growing business.

Every content lesson has a video and printable notes; ten practical projects build your real deliverables, and downloadable templates cover the Business Model Canvas, Business Plan, Financial Model, Pitch Deck and Marketing Plan.

faqs.question: Do I need money to start a business before taking this course?
faqs.answer: No. One of the core lessons is how to validate and start a business with minimal capital. Many successful Liberian businesses started with under $500.

faqs.question: Will this help me access grants?
faqs.answer: Yes. The grant writing module specifically covers major grants available to Liberian entrepreneurs including USAID, World Bank, and Tony Elumelu Foundation programs.

faqs.question: Is this course for people with no business experience?
faqs.answer: This course is designed for everyone from first-time entrepreneurs to experienced business owners wanting to scale. The content is structured to benefit all levels.

faqs.question: How practical is this course?
faqs.answer: Every module includes a hands-on project. By course end you will have a complete business plan, financial projections, pitch deck, and go-to-market strategy, ready for execution.

lessons.title: 1.1 Welcome to the Program
lessons.html:
📖 Welcome to the Program
What this program covers, and what you will have built by the end.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Welcome to the Program

Welcome to the Program is the focus of this Course Orientation lesson. It helps the learner make a practical startup decision, complete an action, and support that action with evidence.

entrepreneur

A person who identifies an opportunity, organises resources, accepts calculated risk, and builds a venture that creates value.

startup

A new venture designed to test and grow a repeatable business model under uncertainty.

validation

The process of collecting real evidence that a problem exists and customers value the proposed solution.

This is a practical entrepreneurship program. It does not teach you to admire successful founders; it walks you through finding a real problem, testing whether anyone will pay to have it solved, and building a business around the answer.

Twenty modules take you from mindset and idea generation, through market research, business models, product, marketing, sales and finance, into funding, legal registration, operations, people, technology and growth. The last modules are practical projects, a startup launch and your capstone.

Key points

  • You will finish with a validated business idea, a business model, a financial plan and a business plan you could take to a lender.
  • Every module asks you to apply the lesson to your own idea, not to a case study.
  • You do not need capital to start this course. You need a problem worth solving and people you can talk to.
  • The examples are drawn from Liberian and West African businesses, because that is the market most learners here will build in.
  • Module 19 contains the practical projects; Module 20 is graduation.

Example

By the end you should be able to say: my customer is this specific group, their problem costs them this much, my solution is this, they will pay this price, I know because I asked twenty of them and eleven committed — and here is the cash flow that shows when the business breaks even.

Why this matters

Most businesses fail for commercial reasons rather than technical ones: they build something nobody wanted, or they run out of cash before revenue arrives. This program is organised around preventing exactly those two failures.

lessons.title: 1.2 How to Study This Course
lessons.html:
📖 How to Study This Course
Getting value out of the program rather than just finishing it.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

How to Study This Course

How to Study This Course is the focus of this Course Orientation lesson. It helps the learner make a practical startup decision, complete an action, and support that action with evidence.

entrepreneur

A person who identifies an opportunity, organises resources, accepts calculated risk, and builds a venture that creates value.

startup

A new venture designed to test and grow a repeatable business model under uncertainty.

validation

The process of collecting real evidence that a problem exists and customers value the proposed solution.

This course is designed to be applied as you go. Each module ends with work on your own idea, and those pieces accumulate into your business plan. Learners who read everything first and apply it at the end finish with knowledge and no business.

The single most important habit is talking to people. Reading about customer discovery teaches you nothing that ten real conversations will not teach you better. Aim to speak to potential customers every single week of this course.

Key points

  • Apply each module to one specific idea, even if you later change it.
  • Talk to at least three potential customers a week, from Module 3 onwards.
  • Keep a single document that grows into your business plan; do not start it in Module 16.
  • Write down what you assumed, then check it — that gap is where learning happens.
  • Expect your idea to change. Changing it because of evidence is progress, not failure.

Example

Two learners take the course. The first completes every lesson and begins her business plan in Module 16 from memory. The second speaks to four customers a week from Module 3 and has ninety recorded conversations by Module 16. Her plan writes itself, and it is grounded in evidence the first has none of.

Why this matters

Entrepreneurship is one of the few subjects where studying without practising produces almost nothing transferable. The habits you build in the first weeks determine what you leave with.

lessons.title: 1.3 What is Entrepreneurship?
lessons.html:
📖 What is Entrepreneurship?
A working definition, and what separates it from simply working for yourself.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

What is Entrepreneurship?

What is Entrepreneurship? is the focus of this Course Orientation lesson. It helps the learner make a practical startup decision, complete an action, and support that action with evidence.

entrepreneur

A person who identifies an opportunity, organises resources, accepts calculated risk, and builds a venture that creates value.

startup

A new venture designed to test and grow a repeatable business model under uncertainty.

validation

The process of collecting real evidence that a problem exists and customers value the proposed solution.

Entrepreneurship is identifying an unmet need and organising resources to meet it, while carrying the risk that you are wrong. The three elements all matter: a need someone will pay to satisfy, resources you assemble rather than already own, and risk you personally bear.

That last element is what distinguishes an entrepreneur from an employee doing the same work. An employee is paid whether the venture succeeds; an entrepreneur is paid only if it does. The reward for carrying that risk is ownership of the upside.

Key points

  • The need must be one people will pay to solve — a problem nobody pays for is a hobby.
  • Resources include money, but also skills, time, relationships and reputation.
  • Risk is not recklessness; skilled entrepreneurs reduce risk deliberately before committing.
  • Entrepreneurship exists inside organisations too, where it is called intrapreneurship.
  • Innovation is common in entrepreneurship but not required — a well-run ordinary business is still entrepreneurship.

Example

Two people open shops selling the same goods on the same street. One simply copies what exists. The other noticed that customers were walking forty minutes to reach the market and opened where they live, cutting their journey. Both are business owners; the second identified an unmet need.

Why this matters

Understanding the definition keeps you focused on the part that creates value: the unmet need. Many new businesses fail because they replicate something already served rather than finding something that is not.

questions.explanation: Meeting an unmet need well is entrepreneurship whether or not the method is novel.

lessons.title: 1.4 What is a Startup?
lessons.html:
📖 What is a Startup?
How a startup differs from a small business, and why the distinction matters.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

What is a Startup?

What is a Startup? is the focus of this Course Orientation lesson. It helps the learner make a practical startup decision, complete an action, and support that action with evidence.

entrepreneur

A person who identifies an opportunity, organises resources, accepts calculated risk, and builds a venture that creates value.

startup

A new venture designed to test and grow a repeatable business model under uncertainty.

validation

The process of collecting real evidence that a problem exists and customers value the proposed solution.

A startup is an organisation searching for a repeatable, scalable business model under conditions of uncertainty. The words searching and scalable carry the meaning. A startup does not yet know what its business model is; it is running experiments to find one.

A small business, by contrast, is executing a known model. A tailor opening a shop knows what tailoring is, who buys it and roughly what it earns. She has real risk, but she is not searching — she is operating.

Key points

  • Startups search for a model; small businesses execute a known one.
  • Scalable means revenue can grow much faster than cost — usually through software, systems or distribution.
  • Most businesses are not startups, and that is not a criticism; small businesses employ most people.
  • The distinction matters for funding: investors fund scalable search, banks fund predictable operation.
  • Choosing the wrong label leads to seeking the wrong kind of money.

Example

A woman selling cooked food from a stall has a small business: the model is known, and doubling revenue means roughly doubling cooking and staff. A woman building an app that connects food sellers to office workers has a startup: she does not yet know if it works, but if it does, serving 5,000 customers costs little more than serving 500.

Why this matters

Many founders seek investment for businesses that are not scalable, and are refused for reasons nobody explains. Knowing which kind of business you have tells you which kind of funding to pursue and what to prove first.

lessons.title: 1.5 Entrepreneur vs. Business Owner
lessons.html:
📖 Entrepreneur vs. Business Owner
Two overlapping roles, and why many people are one without the other.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Entrepreneur vs. Business Owner

Entrepreneur vs. Business Owner is the focus of this Course Orientation lesson. It helps the learner make a practical startup decision, complete an action, and support that action with evidence.

entrepreneur

A person who identifies an opportunity, organises resources, accepts calculated risk, and builds a venture that creates value.

startup

A new venture designed to test and grow a repeatable business model under uncertainty.

validation

The process of collecting real evidence that a problem exists and customers value the proposed solution.

An entrepreneur creates something new: a new offer, a new market, a new way of delivering. A business owner owns and runs a business, which may be entirely conventional. Many people are both, but they are not the same thing.

The practical difference is in what each spends their time on. An entrepreneur spends time discovering — testing whether a need exists and whether a solution works. An owner spends time operating — managing staff, stock, cash and customers. Businesses need both, usually at different stages.

Key points

  • Creation and operation require different skills, and few people are strong at both.
  • Many founders struggle at the transition from discovering to operating.
  • An owner who never innovates is eventually overtaken; an entrepreneur who never operates never gets paid.
  • Recognising which you are good at tells you who to partner with.
  • Both roles are legitimate; the failure is doing one while believing you are doing the other.

Example

A founder builds a delivery service, proves the model and grows it to twelve staff. She is excellent at discovering and poor at scheduling, cash control and staff management. Hiring a manager for operations while she works on the next market is not a retreat; it is matching people to the work.

Why this matters

Knowing which role suits you shapes who you hire, who you partner with, and where you spend your own time. Founders who insist on doing both frequently do neither well.

lessons.title: 1.6 Types of Entrepreneurs
lessons.html:
📖 Types of Entrepreneurs
The main kinds, and what each is actually optimising for.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Types of Entrepreneurs

Types of Entrepreneurs is the focus of this Course Orientation lesson. It helps the learner make a practical startup decision, complete an action, and support that action with evidence.

entrepreneur

A person who identifies an opportunity, organises resources, accepts calculated risk, and builds a venture that creates value.

startup

A new venture designed to test and grow a repeatable business model under uncertainty.

validation

The process of collecting real evidence that a problem exists and customers value the proposed solution.

Entrepreneurs are commonly grouped by what they are trying to achieve. Small business entrepreneurs build a stable enterprise providing a living and employment. Scalable startup entrepreneurs pursue rapid growth and usually take investment. Social entrepreneurs pursue a social or environmental outcome, funded commercially or by donors. Necessity entrepreneurs start businesses because employment is unavailable.

Necessity entrepreneurship is the largest category across West Africa and is often ignored in entrepreneurship teaching, which is written for the scalable startup. Advice designed for a venture-funded startup can be actively harmful to someone whose business must feed a household this month.

Key points

  • Small business: optimises for stability and independence.
  • Scalable startup: optimises for growth, accepting losses early.
  • Social enterprise: optimises for impact, with revenue as the means.
  • Necessity entrepreneurship: optimises for immediate survival income.
  • Advice must match the type — a necessity entrepreneur cannot afford to run at a loss while growing.

Example

A standard startup textbook advises pricing below cost to acquire customers quickly. For a founder whose business must generate household income every week, this advice would be ruinous. The technique is sound for one type and destructive for another.

Why this matters

Identifying your type tells you which advice applies to you and which does not. A great deal of entrepreneurship content assumes a context that does not describe most businesses in this region.

lessons.title: 1.7 Startup Success Stories
lessons.html:
📖 Startup Success Stories
What to learn from successful businesses, and what not to.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Startup Success Stories

Startup Success Stories is the focus of this Course Orientation lesson. It helps the learner make a practical startup decision, complete an action, and support that action with evidence.

entrepreneur

A person who identifies an opportunity, organises resources, accepts calculated risk, and builds a venture that creates value.

startup

A new venture designed to test and grow a repeatable business model under uncertainty.

validation

The process of collecting real evidence that a problem exists and customers value the proposed solution.

Success stories are useful for one thing: showing what a solved problem looks like. They are misleading for almost everything else, because of survivorship bias — we hear about the businesses that worked, not the many that did the same things and failed.

When you read that a founder succeeded by persisting through rejection, remember that thousands who persisted through rejection also failed and were never written about. Persistence did not cause the success; it was necessary but nowhere near sufficient.

Key points

  • Study what problem the business solved and for whom — that part is reliable.
  • Be sceptical of causal claims about founder behaviour; the failures behaved similarly.
  • Local examples teach more than global ones, because the conditions match yours.
  • Ask what the business did in its first year, not what it does now — that is the stage you are at.
  • Failure stories are more instructive than success stories and much rarer.

Example

A mobile money service succeeded in a market where most people had phones but no bank accounts. The transferable lesson is the fit between an existing behaviour and an unmet need. The non-transferable lesson would be to copy its pricing structure into a market with different conditions.

Why this matters

Founders routinely copy the visible surface of successful businesses — the branding, the pricing, the growth tactics — without the underlying fit that made them work. Reading success stories for the problem rather than the tactics is what makes them useful.

lessons.title: 1.8 Course Roadmap
lessons.html:
📖 Course Roadmap
How the twenty modules fit together, and why the order matters.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Course Roadmap

Course Roadmap is the focus of this Course Orientation lesson. It helps the learner make a practical startup decision, complete an action, and support that action with evidence.

entrepreneur

A person who identifies an opportunity, organises resources, accepts calculated risk, and builds a venture that creates value.

startup

A new venture designed to test and grow a repeatable business model under uncertainty.

validation

The process of collecting real evidence that a problem exists and customers value the proposed solution.

The program runs in five stages. Foundation (Modules 1–2) covers what entrepreneurship is and the habits it requires. Discovery (Modules 3–5) is where you find a problem, research the market and design a business model — the most important stage and the one most often rushed.

Building (Modules 6–9) covers product, branding, sales and finance. Resourcing (Modules 10–15) covers funding, legal registration, operations, people, technology and communication. Launch and growth (Modules 16–20) covers planning, launching, growing, the projects and graduation.

Key points

  • The discovery stage determines whether everything after it is worth doing.
  • Do not skip to Module 10 to look for funding before you have evidence anyone wants the product.
  • Each module applies to your own idea; the outputs accumulate into your plan.
  • Finance appears before funding deliberately — you must know your numbers before asking for money.
  • Legal registration comes after validation, so you do not register a business you then abandon.

Example

A founder skips ahead to funding, secures a small loan, and builds a product for eight months. On launch, almost nobody buys, because the problem was assumed rather than tested. The loan must still be repaid. Two weeks of customer interviews in Module 3 would have cost nothing and revealed it.

Why this matters

The order is the accumulated lesson of many failed businesses. Knowing why finance precedes funding, and validation precedes registration, keeps you from spending money and time on a business that was never wanted.

lessons.title: 🛠️ Final Capstone Project
lessons.html:
📖 Final Capstone Project
The brief for the business you will build across the program.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Final Capstone Project

Final Capstone Project is the focus of this Course Orientation lesson. It helps the learner make a practical startup decision, complete an action, and support that action with evidence.

entrepreneur

A person who identifies an opportunity, organises resources, accepts calculated risk, and builds a venture that creates value.

startup

A new venture designed to test and grow a repeatable business model under uncertainty.

validation

The process of collecting real evidence that a problem exists and customers value the proposed solution.

Your capstone is a complete, evidence-backed business plan for one real business idea, built up module by module. It is not written at the end; it is assembled as you go, from work you have actually done.

The idea must be one you could genuinely start. It does not have to be original or ambitious — a small, specific, well-validated business earns a far better capstone than an impressive idea with no evidence behind it.

Key points

  • The problem — who has it, how you know, and what it costs them.
  • Validation evidence — records of customer conversations, with what they said and what they committed to.
  • Business model — a completed canvas with each block justified.
  • Market research — target market, competitors, pricing evidence.
  • Financials — costs, pricing, break-even, monthly cash flow, funding requirement.
  • Operations plan — how the product or service is actually delivered.
  • Risks — the three largest, each with a response.
  • The ask — what you need to start, and what you will do first.

Example

A strong capstone might cover a laundry service for students near a campus: twenty-eight interviews, fourteen who said they would pay a stated price, a measured cost per load, a break-even of eleven customers a week, and a plan to start with one machine and no premises.

Why this matters

This document is what turns the program into something usable. It is what you take to a lender, a partner or a grant committee, and it is the evidence that you can think about a business rather than merely describe one.

lessons.title: 2.1 Developing an Entrepreneurial Mindset
lessons.html:
📖 Developing an Entrepreneurial Mindset
The habits of thought that make entrepreneurship possible.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Developing an Entrepreneurial Mindset

Developing an Entrepreneurial Mindset is the focus of this Entrepreneurial Mindset lesson. It helps the learner make a practical startup decision, complete an action, and support that action with evidence.

entrepreneurial mindset

A way of thinking that looks for opportunities, learns from evidence, and takes responsible action despite uncertainty.

creativity

The ability to generate useful and original ideas, connections, or approaches.

resilience

The ability to recover, learn, and continue after a setback or disappointing result.

An entrepreneurial mindset is a set of habits rather than a personality type. The central one is treating beliefs as assumptions to be tested rather than facts to be defended. A founder who believes customers want something, and goes to find out, is thinking entrepreneurially. One who believes it and builds for a year is not.

The second habit is bias towards action at small scale. Faced with uncertainty, the entrepreneurial response is to design the cheapest test that would settle the question, rather than to research indefinitely or commit fully.

Key points

  • Treat your beliefs as assumptions with a test attached.
  • Prefer a cheap experiment to a long debate.
  • Separate the idea from yourself, so evidence against it is information rather than insult.
  • Look for what would prove you wrong, not what confirms you.
  • Act under uncertainty; waiting for certainty means never starting.

Example

A founder is convinced a delivery service will succeed. Instead of building an app, she posts an offer in three WhatsApp groups and takes orders by phone for two weeks. Eleven people order. She has spent nothing and learned more than eight months of building would have taught her.

Why this matters

Every module after this one depends on this habit. Market research, validation, business models and pricing are all methods for testing assumptions cheaply, and they only work for someone willing to be proved wrong.

lessons.title: 2.2 Creativity and Innovation
lessons.html:
📖 Creativity and Innovation
Producing new options, and turning them into something valuable.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Creativity and Innovation

Creativity and Innovation is the focus of this Entrepreneurial Mindset lesson. It helps the learner make a practical startup decision, complete an action, and support that action with evidence.

entrepreneurial mindset

A way of thinking that looks for opportunities, learns from evidence, and takes responsible action despite uncertainty.

creativity

The ability to generate useful and original ideas, connections, or approaches.

resilience

The ability to recover, learn, and continue after a setback or disappointing result.

Creativity is generating new ideas; innovation is turning one into something people actually use and pay for. They are different activities, and most businesses are stronger at one than the other. An idea nobody adopts is not an innovation, however original.

Creativity is largely a numbers game. Good ideas come from producing many ideas and discarding most, not from waiting for one excellent idea to arrive. The people who appear unusually creative are usually those who generate the most raw material.

Key points

  • Separate generating from judging — evaluating while producing kills output.
  • Combine existing things: most innovation is recombination, not invention from nothing.
  • Change one constraint deliberately — what if it had to cost half as much, or serve one person?
  • Look at how the problem is solved in another industry or another country.
  • Innovation is measured by adoption, not by novelty.

Example

Mobile money was not a new technology. It combined an existing phone network, an existing agent shop network and an existing need to send money. The innovation was the recombination, and its value came entirely from how many people adopted it.

Why this matters

Founders often stall waiting for an original idea. Understanding that most innovation is recombination, and that adoption rather than novelty is the measure, releases you to work with what already exists around you.

lessons.title: 2.3 Identifying Opportunities
lessons.html:
📖 Identifying Opportunities
Where business opportunities actually come from.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Identifying Opportunities

Identifying Opportunities is the focus of this Entrepreneurial Mindset lesson. It helps the learner make a practical startup decision, complete an action, and support that action with evidence.

entrepreneurial mindset

A way of thinking that looks for opportunities, learns from evidence, and takes responsible action despite uncertainty.

creativity

The ability to generate useful and original ideas, connections, or approaches.

resilience

The ability to recover, learn, and continue after a setback or disappointing result.

An opportunity is a gap between what people need and what is available to them, which someone could profitably close. Opportunities are not ideas — an idea is your proposed solution, while the opportunity is the gap itself. Confusing them leads founders to defend a solution after the gap turns out not to exist.

Opportunities cluster in predictable places: where people work around a problem, where they complain repeatedly, where a service exists but is unreliable, where something is available in cities but not in towns, and where a regulation or technology has recently changed.

Key points

  • Watch for workarounds — people improvising a solution is direct evidence of an unmet need.
  • Listen for repeated complaints, especially ones people have stopped expecting to be fixed.
  • Unreliability is an opportunity: an existing service done dependably is often enough.
  • Recent change — a new road, a new regulation, cheaper data — opens gaps that were closed.
  • Your own frustrations are a legitimate starting point, but must still be validated with others.

Example

A founder notices that traders in her market keep photographs of their stock lists on their phones because they have no way to record inventory. The workaround is the signal: they need something enough to improvise a poor version of it themselves.

Why this matters

This is the habit that produces ideas worth pursuing. Most weak business ideas come from imagining what people might want; strong ones come from noticing what people are already struggling to do.

lessons.title: 2.4 Solving Real Problems
lessons.html:
📖 Solving Real Problems
Telling a real problem from an imagined one.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Solving Real Problems

Solving Real Problems is the focus of this Entrepreneurial Mindset lesson. It helps the learner make a practical startup decision, complete an action, and support that action with evidence.

entrepreneurial mindset

A way of thinking that looks for opportunities, learns from evidence, and takes responsible action despite uncertainty.

creativity

The ability to generate useful and original ideas, connections, or approaches.

resilience

The ability to recover, learn, and continue after a setback or disappointing result.

A real problem has three properties: someone specific has it, it costs them something measurable — money, time, risk or discomfort — and they are already doing something about it. The third is the strongest test. People with real problems are already spending money, time or effort trying to solve them.

An imagined problem is one you have reasoned your way to. It usually sounds sensible and nobody is doing anything about it, because it does not hurt enough to act on.

Key points

  • Ask what the person currently does about it — the answer reveals whether it is real.
  • Quantify the cost: how much money, how many hours, how often.
  • 'Nice to have' is a polite way of saying nobody will pay.
  • A problem people pay to solve badly is better than one they do not pay to solve at all.
  • If nobody has tried to solve it and the market is large, ask why — usually the reason matters.

Example

Asked whether they would use a bookkeeping app, twelve shop owners say yes. Asked what they do now, nine say nothing and three keep a notebook. Asked what poor records have cost them, eight cannot name anything. The stated interest was real; the problem was not.

Why this matters

This single question — what do you do about it now — separates businesses worth building from ideas that interview well and sell nothing. It is the most useful question in this entire program.

lessons.title: 2.5 Growth Mindset
lessons.html:
📖 Growth Mindset
Treating ability as something built rather than fixed.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Growth Mindset

Growth Mindset is the focus of this Entrepreneurial Mindset lesson. It helps the learner make a practical startup decision, complete an action, and support that action with evidence.

entrepreneurial mindset

A way of thinking that looks for opportunities, learns from evidence, and takes responsible action despite uncertainty.

creativity

The ability to generate useful and original ideas, connections, or approaches.

resilience

The ability to recover, learn, and continue after a setback or disappointing result.

A growth mindset is the belief that ability is developed through effort and feedback rather than fixed at birth. In entrepreneurship this matters more than in most fields, because the work consists largely of doing things you have not done before and doing them badly at first.

The practical consequence is how you interpret failure. With a fixed mindset, a failed sales call means you are not good at selling. With a growth mindset it means that approach did not work, and the useful question is what to change.

Key points

  • Interpret failure as information about the approach, not about your capacity.
  • Seek feedback deliberately, especially from people likely to disagree.
  • Learn in public — asking questions early costs less than pretending to know.
  • Track what you could not do six months ago; it is the evidence that ability moves.
  • Distinguish persistence from stubbornness: persist with the goal, change the method.

Example

A founder's first ten sales calls all fail. Rather than concluding she cannot sell, she asks the last three why they declined. Two say the price was unclear. She rewrites the offer, and the next ten calls produce three sales.

Why this matters

Entrepreneurship involves a high rate of visible failure, and how you interpret it determines whether you continue. The distinction between persisting with the goal and persisting with a failing method is what separates useful determination from waste.

lessons.title: 2.6 Leadership Skills
lessons.html:
📖 Leadership Skills
Getting work done through others when you cannot pay much.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Leadership Skills

Leadership Skills is the focus of this Entrepreneurial Mindset lesson. It helps the learner make a practical startup decision, complete an action, and support that action with evidence.

entrepreneurial mindset

A way of thinking that looks for opportunities, learns from evidence, and takes responsible action despite uncertainty.

creativity

The ability to generate useful and original ideas, connections, or approaches.

resilience

The ability to recover, learn, and continue after a setback or disappointing result.

Early-stage founders lead without the usual tools. There is little money, no established reputation and often no formal authority over the people whose help you need — partners, suppliers, early staff, family who are lending you time.

What remains is clarity and reliability. People follow a founder who can explain plainly where the business is going and who consistently does what they said. Both are within your control from day one and cost nothing.

Key points

  • Be able to state in two sentences what the business does and why it matters.
  • Do what you said you would do, or say early that you cannot.
  • Give people responsibility for outcomes, not just tasks.
  • Handle mistakes by fixing the system, not by finding someone to blame.
  • Pay people what you promised, on time, before you pay yourself.

Example

A founder cannot yet pay a designer market rate. She explains exactly what the business is, what the designer's work will make possible, agrees a reduced fee with a share of the first month's revenue, and pays on the agreed day. The designer stays with the business for three years.

Why this matters

Almost everything a founder achieves early on depends on people helping for less than they are worth. That help is bought with clarity and kept with reliability, and both are habits rather than resources.

lessons.title: 2.7 Decision Making
lessons.html:
📖 Decision Making
Deciding well under uncertainty and time pressure.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Decision Making

Decision Making is the focus of this Entrepreneurial Mindset lesson. It helps the learner make a practical startup decision, complete an action, and support that action with evidence.

entrepreneurial mindset

A way of thinking that looks for opportunities, learns from evidence, and takes responsible action despite uncertainty.

creativity

The ability to generate useful and original ideas, connections, or approaches.

resilience

The ability to recover, learn, and continue after a setback or disappointing result.

Founders make many decisions with incomplete information. The useful skill is not making the right decision every time; it is matching the effort you spend to what the decision is worth and whether it can be undone.

Sort decisions by two questions: how costly is it if wrong, and can it be reversed? Reversible, low-cost decisions should be made fast — the cost of deliberating exceeds the cost of being wrong. Irreversible, expensive decisions deserve real analysis and, where possible, a small test first.

Key points

  • Decide fast on reversible things; slowly on irreversible ones.
  • Ask what you would need to know to decide, then find out if it is cheap to find out.
  • Set a deadline for the decision; open decisions consume attention indefinitely.
  • Write down the reasoning, so you can later judge the decision separately from the outcome.
  • A good decision can have a bad outcome; do not learn the wrong lesson from luck.

Example

Choosing a supplier for a first small order is reversible and cheap — decide today. Signing a two-year lease on premises is neither. The second deserves a month of work and, if possible, a short sublet first to test the location.

Why this matters

Founders lose enormous time deliberating over small reversible choices while committing quickly to large irreversible ones. Sorting by cost and reversibility corrects both errors at once.

questions.explanation: A cheap test converts an irreversible commitment into an informed one.

lessons.title: 2.8 Critical Thinking
lessons.html:
📖 Critical Thinking
Examining claims, including your own, before acting on them.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Critical Thinking

Critical Thinking is the focus of this Entrepreneurial Mindset lesson. It helps the learner make a practical startup decision, complete an action, and support that action with evidence.

entrepreneurial mindset

A way of thinking that looks for opportunities, learns from evidence, and takes responsible action despite uncertainty.

creativity

The ability to generate useful and original ideas, connections, or approaches.

resilience

The ability to recover, learn, and continue after a setback or disappointing result.

Critical thinking means checking whether a conclusion actually follows from the evidence. For founders the claims most in need of checking are their own, because nobody else has as much reason to believe them.

The recurring errors are predictable. Confirmation bias makes you notice supporting evidence and overlook the rest. Small samples from friendly people feel like validation. Correlation gets read as cause. And anecdote from one enthusiastic customer gets treated as a market.

Key points

  • Ask what evidence would change your mind, and then look for it.
  • Count who you asked and who you did not; friends and family are not a sample.
  • Distinguish what someone said from what they did; behaviour is the stronger evidence.
  • Beware conclusions that happen to be convenient for you.
  • Ask 'compared to what?' — a number alone rarely means anything.

Example

A founder reports that 80 percent of people she surveyed would buy her product. She surveyed ten people, eight of whom were friends who knew it was her idea. The figure is arithmetically correct and tells her nothing about the market.

Why this matters

Almost every expensive founder mistake involves believing something on evidence that would not have survived a simple check. These few habits catch most of them, and they cost nothing to apply.

questions.explanation: A figure only carries meaning against a baseline or an alternative.

lessons.title: 2.9 Time Management
lessons.html:
📖 Time Management
Spending your hours on what actually moves the business.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Time Management

Time Management is the focus of this Entrepreneurial Mindset lesson. It helps the learner make a practical startup decision, complete an action, and support that action with evidence.

entrepreneurial mindset

A way of thinking that looks for opportunities, learns from evidence, and takes responsible action despite uncertainty.

creativity

The ability to generate useful and original ideas, connections, or approaches.

resilience

The ability to recover, learn, and continue after a setback or disappointing result.

Founders have more possible work than time, permanently. Time management is therefore not about efficiency — doing more things faster — but about selection: deciding which things not to do.

The reliable filter is to ask which activity most reduces the biggest current uncertainty. Early on that is almost always talking to customers, and it is almost always the activity founders avoid in favour of visible, comfortable work like designing a logo or building a website.

Key points

  • Identify the biggest current uncertainty, and spend your best hours reducing it.
  • Beware comfortable work: tasks that feel productive but resolve nothing.
  • Batch similar tasks; switching between kinds of work is where hours disappear.
  • Protect a block of uninterrupted time for the hardest task, early in the day.
  • Say no explicitly; unanswered requests consume attention until they are closed.

Example

A founder spends three weeks perfecting a logo and website before launch. The business had never confirmed anyone would pay. Those three weeks spent on customer conversations would have revealed that the price was double what the market would bear — before any of the design work mattered.

Why this matters

How a founder spends the first months usually determines whether the business survives. Comfortable work is the commonest way to spend that time without learning anything, and recognising it is the defence.

lessons.title: 2.10 Personal Productivity
lessons.html:
📖 Personal Productivity
Systems that keep work moving when nobody is supervising you.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Personal Productivity

Personal Productivity is the focus of this Entrepreneurial Mindset lesson. It helps the learner make a practical startup decision, complete an action, and support that action with evidence.

entrepreneurial mindset

A way of thinking that looks for opportunities, learns from evidence, and takes responsible action despite uncertainty.

creativity

The ability to generate useful and original ideas, connections, or approaches.

resilience

The ability to recover, learn, and continue after a setback or disappointing result.

Nobody assigns a founder their work. Productivity therefore depends on having a system rather than on motivation, because motivation is unreliable and a system is not.

A workable system needs three parts: a single place where every commitment is captured, a weekly review where you decide what matters next, and a short daily list of things that will actually be done. The commonest failure is a list so long it is ignored, which returns you to working on whatever feels urgent.

Key points

  • Capture every commitment in one place, immediately; memory is not a system.
  • Review weekly: what moved, what did not, and what matters most next week.
  • Keep the daily list to three things you will genuinely finish.
  • Distinguish urgent from important; urgency is often someone else's priority.
  • Schedule rest deliberately — exhaustion produces bad decisions, which are expensive.

Example

A founder keeps commitments in her head, in messages and on scraps of paper. She misses a supplier callback and a customer follow-up in the same week. Moving everything into one notebook with a Sunday review costs twenty minutes and both failures stop.

Why this matters

Founders fail more often from dropped commitments than from bad strategy, and dropped commitments damage exactly the reliability that early leadership depends on. A simple system protects it.

lessons.title: 3.1 Finding Business Ideas
lessons.html:
📖 Finding Business Ideas
Where to look, systematically, rather than waiting for inspiration.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Finding Business Ideas

Finding Business Ideas is the focus of this Idea Generation & Validation lesson. It helps the learner make a practical startup decision, complete an action, and support that action with evidence.

problem

A difficulty, unmet need, or costly frustration experienced by a specific group of people.

customer discovery

Structured conversations and observation used to understand customers before building a solution.

idea validation

Testing the main assumptions behind a business idea with evidence from real potential customers.

Business ideas are found by looking in specific places rather than by waiting. The most productive sources are your own work experience, the frustrations of people you know well, industries undergoing change, and things that exist elsewhere but not here.

Your existing knowledge matters more than originality. An idea in a field you understand gives you an advantage in judging whether it is real, who the customer is and what it costs to deliver. An idea in a field you know nothing about requires you to learn all of that before you can even evaluate it.

Key points

  • Start from what you know: the industry you worked in, the community you belong to.
  • Ask ten people what wasted their time or money this week.
  • Look at what exists in Accra or Lagos but not yet in Monrovia, and ask why.
  • Watch for recent change — new roads, cheaper data, new regulation — which opens gaps.
  • Keep an idea list; write down every candidate without judging it at the time.

Example

A former hospital clerk notices that patients repeatedly lose paper referral letters and must repeat tests. She knows the system, the staff and the constraints. That knowledge is worth more than a more impressive idea in an industry she has never worked in.

Why this matters

Founders frequently discard their most valuable asset — their own experience — in favour of ideas that sound more exciting. Ideas grounded in what you already understand are validated faster and executed better.

lessons.title: 3.2 Problem Identification
lessons.html:
📖 Problem Identification
Stating the problem precisely enough to test it.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Problem Identification

Problem Identification is the focus of this Idea Generation & Validation lesson. It helps the learner make a practical startup decision, complete an action, and support that action with evidence.

problem

A difficulty, unmet need, or costly frustration experienced by a specific group of people.

customer discovery

Structured conversations and observation used to understand customers before building a solution.

idea validation

Testing the main assumptions behind a business idea with evidence from real potential customers.

A problem statement should name who has the problem, what the problem is in observable terms, how often it occurs and what it costs them. Vague statements cannot be tested, and untestable statements let a founder proceed on assumption indefinitely.

Compare small businesses struggle with finances against shop owners in Red Light market cannot tell which products are profitable, because they record all sales as one daily total, and they discover slow-moving stock only when it expires. The second names a person, a mechanism and a cost. It can be checked.

Key points

  • Name a specific person or group, not a category like 'small businesses'.
  • Describe the problem as something observable, not as a lack of your solution.
  • State frequency: daily, weekly, once a season.
  • Quantify the cost in money, time or risk.
  • Never write the problem as 'they do not have X' where X is your product.

Example

A founder writes: the problem is that farmers do not have an app for record keeping. This is not a problem statement; it is a description of a missing product. The actual problem might be that farmers cannot tell which plot is losing money — and an app is only one possible response to it.

Why this matters

Every later stage — validation, model, pricing, marketing — depends on the problem statement. A problem defined as the absence of your product cannot be disproved, so the whole business proceeds untested.

lessons.title: 3.3 Brainstorming Techniques
lessons.html:
📖 Brainstorming Techniques
Producing many options before choosing one.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Brainstorming Techniques

Brainstorming Techniques is the focus of this Idea Generation & Validation lesson. It helps the learner make a practical startup decision, complete an action, and support that action with evidence.

problem

A difficulty, unmet need, or costly frustration experienced by a specific group of people.

customer discovery

Structured conversations and observation used to understand customers before building a solution.

idea validation

Testing the main assumptions behind a business idea with evidence from real potential customers.

Brainstorming is generating a large number of candidate solutions without evaluating them. The rule that makes it work is deferring judgement: as soon as ideas are criticised, output collapses and people offer only safe suggestions.

Volume is the aim. The first ideas produced are usually the obvious ones everybody has; useful ideas tend to appear after the obvious ones are exhausted, which is why stopping early defeats the purpose.

Key points

  • Set a target number — thirty ideas — and reach it before evaluating any.
  • Write ideas individually first, then share; groups converge too early otherwise.
  • Build on others' ideas rather than replacing them.
  • Use prompts: what if it were free, what if it served one person, what if it were illegal to do it the current way.
  • Evaluate in a separate session, against criteria agreed beforehand.

Example

A group asked to improve a delivery service produces six ideas in five minutes, all variations on faster bikes. Pushed to reach thirty, they eventually propose collecting orders at a fixed pickup point — which turns out to be cheaper and more reliable than any delivery improvement.

Why this matters

Founders routinely commit to their first idea, which is usually the obvious one their competitors also had. Generating properly before choosing is a cheap way to find the option nobody else considered.

lessons.title: 3.4 Market Gap Analysis
lessons.html:
📖 Market Gap Analysis
Finding what is missing between what exists and what people need.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Market Gap Analysis

Market Gap Analysis is the focus of this Idea Generation & Validation lesson. It helps the learner make a practical startup decision, complete an action, and support that action with evidence.

problem

A difficulty, unmet need, or costly frustration experienced by a specific group of people.

customer discovery

Structured conversations and observation used to understand customers before building a solution.

idea validation

Testing the main assumptions behind a business idea with evidence from real potential customers.

A market gap is a need that current offerings do not meet. Gaps appear in four forms: a segment nobody serves, a price point nobody occupies, a quality or reliability level nobody delivers, and a location or time nobody covers.

Finding one requires mapping what already exists honestly. Founders frequently claim there is no competition, which almost always means they have not looked. Whatever the customer does now — including doing nothing, or improvising — is the competition.

Key points

  • List every existing option, including informal ones and doing nothing.
  • For each, note who it serves, at what price, at what quality, where and when.
  • The gap is where a group of customers fits none of the existing options.
  • Time and location gaps are the most common and the most overlooked.
  • 'No competition' usually means the market has been surveyed carelessly, or nobody wants it.

Example

Mapping laundry options near a campus reveals three shops, all closed by 6pm and none collecting. Students finish classes at 5.30 and work evenings. The gap is not a missing service — it is a missing time and a missing collection, which requires no new capability at all.

Why this matters

Gap analysis converts a vague sense of opportunity into a specific, defensible position. It also tests honesty: a founder who cannot name what customers do today has not done the work.

lessons.title: 3.5 Design Thinking
lessons.html:
📖 Design Thinking
A method for designing around the user rather than around the idea.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Design Thinking

Design Thinking is the focus of this Idea Generation & Validation lesson. It helps the learner make a practical startup decision, complete an action, and support that action with evidence.

problem

A difficulty, unmet need, or costly frustration experienced by a specific group of people.

customer discovery

Structured conversations and observation used to understand customers before building a solution.

idea validation

Testing the main assumptions behind a business idea with evidence from real potential customers.

Design thinking is a five-stage process: empathise with the user, define the problem from their perspective, ideate possible responses, prototype cheaply, and test with real users. It then loops.

Its value for founders is that it forces the problem definition to come from the user rather than from the founder's assumption. The empathise stage is not a courtesy; it is where you discover that the problem you imagined is not the problem people have.

Key points

  • Empathise by observing what people do, not only by asking what they think.
  • Define the problem in the user's words, from what you observed.
  • Prototype at the lowest fidelity that can be tested — paper, a message, a manual service.
  • Test with people who would actually use it, not with friends.
  • Expect to loop; the first definition is usually wrong.

Example

A founder designing a market inventory tool sits with three traders for a morning. She sees that they cannot stop serving customers to record anything, which rules out the app she imagined. The workable prototype turns out to be an end-of-day photograph of the stall, reviewed later.

Why this matters

Observation regularly overturns assumptions that survey questions confirm. Watching how people actually work is the cheapest correction available, and it happens before any money is spent building.

lessons.title: 3.6 Customer Discovery
lessons.html:
📖 Customer Discovery
Going out to find out who the customer is and what they need.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Customer Discovery

Customer Discovery is the focus of this Idea Generation & Validation lesson. It helps the learner make a practical startup decision, complete an action, and support that action with evidence.

problem

A difficulty, unmet need, or costly frustration experienced by a specific group of people.

customer discovery

Structured conversations and observation used to understand customers before building a solution.

idea validation

Testing the main assumptions behind a business idea with evidence from real potential customers.

Customer discovery is the systematic process of leaving your desk and testing your assumptions with real people. It has one rule: you are gathering information, not selling. The moment you begin persuading, you stop learning, because people stop telling you what they think.

The questions that work are about the past and the present. What did you do the last time this happened? How much did it cost you? What did you try before? Questions about the future — would you use this, would you pay — produce polite answers that predict nothing.

Key points

  • Ask about specific past behaviour, not hypothetical future behaviour.
  • Do not describe your solution until the end, if at all.
  • Listen for what they already spend money or effort on.
  • Talk to people outside your circle; friends protect your feelings.
  • Record what was said, verbatim where possible, immediately afterwards.
  • Twenty conversations is a reasonable minimum before drawing conclusions.

Example

Instead of asking would you pay for a delivery service, a founder asks tell me about the last time you needed something delivered. She learns that three of eight had paid a motorbike rider that month, what they paid, and that the failure was riders not showing up. None of that would have come from the first question.

Why this matters

This is the single highest-value activity in the entire program. It costs nothing but time, it can begin today, and it is the only way to find out whether the business you are planning has a customer.

lessons.title: 3.7 Customer Interviews
lessons.html:
📖 Customer Interviews
Running an interview that produces evidence rather than encouragement.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Customer Interviews

Customer Interviews is the focus of this Idea Generation & Validation lesson. It helps the learner make a practical startup decision, complete an action, and support that action with evidence.

problem

A difficulty, unmet need, or costly frustration experienced by a specific group of people.

customer discovery

Structured conversations and observation used to understand customers before building a solution.

idea validation

Testing the main assumptions behind a business idea with evidence from real potential customers.

An interview is a structured conversation with a purpose. Prepare five to seven open questions, ask them in a consistent order across interviews so answers can be compared, and let the person talk far more than you do.

The commonest mistakes are leading questions, which suggest the answer you want, and pitching, which turns the interview into a sales call. Don't you find it frustrating when deliveries are late? teaches you nothing; walk me through your last delivery teaches you a great deal.

Key points

  • Prepare open questions beginning with what, how, when, tell me about.
  • Ask the same core questions every time, so you can compare across interviews.
  • Follow up on anything surprising — that is where the value usually is.
  • Aim to speak less than a quarter of the time.
  • Close by asking who else you should speak to, and whether you may follow up.
  • Write up within an hour, while you still remember the wording.

Example

Across twenty interviews a founder asks the same question about the last purchase in this category. Fourteen mention the same specific frustration unprompted. That consistency, across a comparable set of questions, is evidence. One enthusiastic conversation would not have been.

Why this matters

Comparability is what turns conversations into data. Asking the same questions in the same way is what lets you say fourteen of twenty rather than 'people seem to think'.

lessons.title: 3.8 Idea Validation
lessons.html:
📖 Idea Validation
Establishing that people will actually pay, before you build.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Idea Validation

Idea Validation is the focus of this Idea Generation & Validation lesson. It helps the learner make a practical startup decision, complete an action, and support that action with evidence.

problem

A difficulty, unmet need, or costly frustration experienced by a specific group of people.

customer discovery

Structured conversations and observation used to understand customers before building a solution.

idea validation

Testing the main assumptions behind a business idea with evidence from real potential customers.

Validation means obtaining evidence that people will part with money for your solution. Interest is not validation. Praise is not validation. The evidence that counts is a commitment: a deposit, a pre-order, a signed agreement, or at minimum a specific promise attached to a date and a price.

The reason is straightforward. Saying yes costs nothing, so it predicts nothing. Handing over money, or agreeing to a specific transaction, costs something — and that cost is what makes it evidence.

Key points

  • Rank evidence by what it costs the customer: payment, deposit, signed order, scheduled commitment, verbal interest, praise.
  • Sell before you build wherever possible; a pre-order validates and funds simultaneously.
  • A concierge test — delivering the service manually for a few customers — validates without any product.
  • Define in advance what result would count as validated, and what would not.
  • Refusals are data; record why people said no.

Example

A founder offers her planned service by message to thirty people at a stated price, asking for a small deposit to reserve a slot. Four pay. That is weak demand at that price — but it is real information, obtained in a week, before anything was built.

Why this matters

Building before validating is the most expensive mistake in entrepreneurship, and it is nearly always avoidable. Almost every business idea can be tested in some form within two weeks and for very little money.

questions.explanation: Only evidence with a cost attached predicts actual purchasing behaviour.

To measure market size

questions.explanation: Why people decline usually explains what is wrong with the price, the offer or the target.

lessons.title: 3.9 Product-Market Fit
lessons.html:
📖 Product-Market Fit
What it is, and how you can tell whether you have it.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Product-Market Fit

Product-Market Fit is the focus of this Idea Generation & Validation lesson. It helps the learner make a practical startup decision, complete an action, and support that action with evidence.

problem

A difficulty, unmet need, or costly frustration experienced by a specific group of people.

customer discovery

Structured conversations and observation used to understand customers before building a solution.

idea validation

Testing the main assumptions behind a business idea with evidence from real potential customers.

Product-market fit is the state where a product satisfies a real need for a definable group of customers, well enough that they keep using it and tell others. It is the point before which growth spending is wasted and after which it is worthwhile.

The signals are behavioural rather than emotional. Customers return without being prompted. They refer others. They complain when the service is unavailable, which means it has become part of how they operate. Absence of fit looks like customers who say pleasant things and never come back.

Key points

  • Retention is the clearest signal: do customers come back on their own?
  • Referral without prompting indicates real value.
  • Complaints during an outage are a positive signal — it means they depend on you.
  • Do not scale before fit; growth spending on a leaky product multiplies the leak.
  • Fit is for a specific segment; you may have it with one group and not another.

Example

A service has 200 sign-ups and 12 weekly active users, most of whom message the founder directly when something breaks. The 200 is vanity; the 12 who depend on it are the beginning of fit, and understanding what those 12 have in common defines the segment to pursue.

Why this matters

Founders commonly spend on marketing before they have fit, which increases the number of people who try the product and leave. Knowing the behavioural signals tells you when spending will compound rather than evaporate.

options: Investor interest

questions.explanation: Repeat use is behaviour, and behaviour predicts value where opinion does not.

questions.explanation: Acquiring more customers for a product that does not retain them wastes the acquisition cost.

lessons.title: 3.10 Selecting the Best Business Idea
lessons.html:
📖 Selecting the Best Business Idea
Choosing between candidates on criteria set in advance.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Selecting the Best Business Idea

Selecting the Best Business Idea is the focus of this Idea Generation & Validation lesson. It helps the learner make a practical startup decision, complete an action, and support that action with evidence.

problem

A difficulty, unmet need, or costly frustration experienced by a specific group of people.

customer discovery

Structured conversations and observation used to understand customers before building a solution.

idea validation

Testing the main assumptions behind a business idea with evidence from real potential customers.

By this point you should have several candidate ideas. Choosing between them works best against criteria agreed before you look at the options, because deciding the criteria afterwards means choosing the idea you already preferred and justifying it.

Useful criteria for a first business are: strength of evidence that the problem is real, your own ability to deliver it, how quickly it could generate revenue, how much capital it needs to start, and how cheaply it can be tested further.

Key points

  • Score each idea against the same criteria; do not evaluate them one at a time.
  • Weight evidence of demand most heavily — it is the factor most often assumed.
  • Prefer ideas you can start small and cheaply, especially for a first business.
  • Consider time to first revenue; long pre-revenue periods require funding you may not have.
  • Be honest about your own capability; enthusiasm is not a substitute for skill or access.

Example

Three ideas are scored. The most exciting requires $4,000 and six months before any revenue. The least exciting requires $150, can begin next week and already has four people who have paid deposits. For a first business, the second is the better choice on every criterion that matters.

Why this matters

The idea you start with is less important than getting into the market and learning. Choosing the one that can be tested cheapest and fastest usually teaches you more than choosing the one that sounds most impressive.

lessons.title: 4.1 Introduction to Market Research
lessons.html:
📖 Introduction to Market Research
What market research answers, and what it cannot.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Introduction to Market Research

Introduction to Market Research is the focus of this Market Research lesson. It helps the learner make a practical startup decision, complete an action, and support that action with evidence.

primary research

New information collected directly from people through interviews, surveys, observation, or experiments.

secondary research

Existing information gathered from reports, databases, publications, and credible online sources.

target market

The defined group of customers a business chooses to serve.

Market research is the systematic gathering of information about customers, competitors and market conditions so that decisions rest on evidence. It answers four questions: who the customer is, how many there are, what they currently do, and what they will pay.

What it cannot do is tell you whether people will buy something that does not yet exist. Stated intention is unreliable, so research narrows and informs; only a real transaction validates. Treat research as reducing uncertainty rather than removing it.

Key points

  • Define the decision the research will inform before you start gathering.
  • Cheap research first: observation, existing data, conversations. Surveys later, if at all.
  • Sample size matters less than sample relevance; ten real customers beat a hundred strangers.
  • Research informs; a transaction validates.
  • Record where every figure came from, so it can be checked later.

Example

A founder spends six weeks producing a 40-page market report estimating a large addressable market. None of it establishes whether anyone will pay her price. Two weeks of customer conversations and one paid pilot would have been worth more than the entire report.

Why this matters

Research is easy to hide in, because it feels productive and involves no rejection. Defining the decision first keeps it proportionate and prevents it becoming a substitute for talking to customers.

options: Whether people will actually buy something that does not yet exist

options: Number of questions

questions.question: What should be defined before research begins?
options: The budget
The sample size

The report format
questions.explanation: Without a decision in view, research expands indefinitely and answers nothing.

lessons.title: 4.2 Primary Research
lessons.html:
📖 Primary Research
Information you gather yourself, directly from the source.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Primary Research

Primary Research is the focus of this Market Research lesson. It helps the learner make a practical startup decision, complete an action, and support that action with evidence.

primary research

New information collected directly from people through interviews, surveys, observation, or experiments.

secondary research

Existing information gathered from reports, databases, publications, and credible online sources.

target market

The defined group of customers a business chooses to serve.

Primary research is data you collect for your specific question: interviews, observation, surveys, experiments and pilot sales. Its advantage is that it is exactly about your market, your customers and your offer. Its cost is your time.

For a founder, the highest-value primary methods are conversation and observation, because they surface things you did not know to ask about. Surveys only capture answers to questions you already thought of, which makes them useful for measuring, not for discovering.

Key points

  • Interviews and observation for discovery; surveys for measuring something you already understand.
  • Observe where possible — people describe their behaviour inaccurately.
  • A pilot sale is primary research and validation at the same time.
  • Go where your customers already are rather than recruiting them to you.
  • Keep raw notes; summaries lose the detail you will need later.

Example

A founder wants to know how traders manage stock. A survey would ask 'how do you record stock?' and receive tidy answers. Spending a morning at three stalls shows her that records are made at closing time, hurriedly, on the back of receipts — which changes what she needs to build.

Why this matters

Primary research is where founders acquire the specific knowledge competitors lack. It is also the part most often skipped in favour of secondary research, which is more comfortable and much less useful.

lessons.title: 4.3 Secondary Research
lessons.html:
📖 Secondary Research
Using information someone else already gathered.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Secondary Research

Secondary Research is the focus of this Market Research lesson. It helps the learner make a practical startup decision, complete an action, and support that action with evidence.

primary research

New information collected directly from people through interviews, surveys, observation, or experiments.

secondary research

Existing information gathered from reports, databases, publications, and credible online sources.

target market

The defined group of customers a business chooses to serve.

Secondary research uses existing sources: government statistics, industry reports, census data, trade association figures, news, and competitors' published material. It is fast and usually free, which makes it a sensible starting point.

Its limitations are specific. The data was collected for someone else's purpose, it may be out of date, and it may cover a different geography or population than yours. National figures in particular can be badly misleading for a business operating in one town.

Key points

  • Check the date and the geography of any figure before using it.
  • Note who produced it and why — industry bodies and vendors have interests.
  • National averages rarely describe a single town or neighbourhood.
  • Use secondary research to frame questions, then answer them with primary research.
  • Cite the source of every number in your plan; unsourced figures are not evidence.

Example

A national statistic reports average household spending on a category. The founder's actual customers are students in one district, whose spending bears no relation to the national average. The figure is accurate and irrelevant, and using it would produce a revenue forecast that cannot happen.

Why this matters

Secondary research gives you context cheaply and quickly, and it makes your plan credible when sourced properly. Treating it as a substitute for talking to your actual customers is where it goes wrong.

questions.explanation: It provides context cheaply, but the specific answers must come from your own market.

lessons.title: 4.4 Customer Personas
lessons.html:
📖 Customer Personas
Building a concrete picture of the person you are actually serving.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Customer Personas

Customer Personas is the focus of this Market Research lesson. It helps the learner make a practical startup decision, complete an action, and support that action with evidence.

primary research

New information collected directly from people through interviews, surveys, observation, or experiments.

secondary research

Existing information gathered from reports, databases, publications, and credible online sources.

target market

The defined group of customers a business chooses to serve.

A persona is a detailed, semi-fictional profile of one representative customer, built from real interviews rather than imagination. It exists to keep every later decision — product, pricing, marketing wording — anchored to a specific person instead of a vague crowd.

A useful persona names who they are, what their day looks like, what frustrates them about the problem you address, what they have tried before, and what would make them trust a new provider. A persona invented at a desk, with no interviews behind it, is a guess wearing a name.

Key points

  • Base every detail on something an actual interviewee said or did.
  • Include the specific frustration and what they currently do about it.
  • One well-built persona beats five vague ones covering everyone.
  • Revisit and revise the persona as you interview more people.
  • Use it as a test: would this specific person buy what you are building?

Example

A founder building a bookkeeping tool writes a persona for Comfort, who runs a provision shop, records sales on paper because she closes late and is too tired to type into an app, and has tried and abandoned two apps that needed daily data entry. That single detail redirects the whole design towards low-effort, end-of-day capture.

Why this matters

Teams that skip personas end up designing for an imagined average customer who does not exist, and are then surprised when real customers behave differently. A persona grounded in interviews keeps the whole team building for someone real.
