lessons.title: 4.5 Target Market
lessons.html:
📖 Target Market
Defining who you are actually selling to, precisely enough to reach them.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Target Market

Target Market is the focus of this Market Research lesson. It helps the learner make a practical startup decision, complete an action, and support that action with evidence.

primary research

New information collected directly from people through interviews, surveys, observation, or experiments.

secondary research

Existing information gathered from reports, databases, publications, and credible online sources.

target market

The defined group of customers a business chooses to serve.

A target market is the specific group of customers a business focuses on, defined narrowly enough that you can find them, understand them, and reach them with a consistent message. 'Everyone' is not a target market; it describes a business with no way to focus its limited resources.

Defining it narrowly at the start does not mean staying narrow forever. It means picking a starting point specific enough to learn from, then expanding once that first segment is understood and served well.

Key points

  • Define by a combination of who they are, where they are, and what specific need they have.
  • A narrow, reachable segment beats a broad, vague one for a new business.
  • Check that the segment is large enough to sustain the business before committing.
  • Different segments often need different messages, pricing or channels.
  • Expansion to new segments should follow evidence, not hope.

Example

A tutoring startup initially defines its market as 'students.' Refined to 'WASSCE candidates in Monrovia retaking mathematics,' it becomes possible to find them (through specific schools and past-candidate networks), understand their specific fear (failing the retake), and reach them with one focused message.

Why this matters

A precise target market is what makes marketing affordable for a small business. A vague one means paying to reach many people who were never going to buy, which a new business usually cannot afford.

lessons.title: 📝 Practice: Target Market
lessons.html: Quick check: Review the notes and complete the two action steps, then answer these to confirm you understood Target Market.

questions.question: Why is 'everyone' not a usable target market?
options: It gives no way to focus limited resources or craft one message
It is illegal to target everyone
Everyone already has a preferred provider
It is too expensive to reach everyone
questions.explanation: Without a defined focus, marketing spend and product decisions have nothing to aim at.

questions.question: Why start with a narrow target market?
options: Narrow markets are always larger
It is specific enough to learn from and serve well before expanding
Regulations require narrow targeting
Narrow markets need no marketing
questions.explanation: A focused starting segment can be understood and reached; expansion follows once it is proven.

questions.question: What must be checked before committing to a narrow segment?
options: That the segment is the cheapest to reach
That competitors are absent
That the segment is large enough to sustain the business
That the segment has no existing habits
questions.explanation: A segment defined too narrowly may not contain enough customers to build a viable business.

lessons.title: 4.6 Industry Analysis
lessons.html:
📖 Industry Analysis
Understanding the wider forces shaping every business in your space.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Industry Analysis

Industry Analysis is the focus of this Market Research lesson. It helps the learner make a practical startup decision, complete an action, and support that action with evidence.

primary research

New information collected directly from people through interviews, surveys, observation, or experiments.

secondary research

Existing information gathered from reports, databases, publications, and credible online sources.

target market

The defined group of customers a business chooses to serve.

Industry analysis looks beyond your specific competitors to the forces shaping the whole sector: how big it is, whether it is growing or shrinking, how it is regulated, and what technology or behaviour is changing it.

This matters because a good business idea in a shrinking or heavily disrupted industry can still fail, while a mediocre idea in a growing industry with rising demand can still succeed. Industry conditions set the current a business is swimming with or against.

Key points

  • Establish whether the industry is growing, stable or shrinking, and why.
  • Identify regulatory requirements before committing capital.
  • Watch for technology or behaviour shifts that are changing how the industry works.
  • Consider how easily new competitors can enter — low barriers mean constant new competition.
  • An unattractive industry does not rule out a business, but it changes what success requires.

Example

A founder plans a DVD rental shop just as streaming becomes affordable and widespread in the target city. The business concept is executed well, but the industry itself is disappearing under it, and no amount of local execution can offset that current.

Why this matters

Assessing the industry protects a founder from betting effort and capital against a current that is stronger than any one business can fight, and helps identify sectors where growth makes even average execution rewarding.

lessons.title: 📝 Practice: Industry Analysis
lessons.html: Quick check: Review the notes and complete the two action steps, then answer these to confirm you understood Industry Analysis.

questions.question: What can happen to a good business idea in a shrinking industry?
options: Shrinking industries have no competition
It becomes exempt from regulation
It automatically succeeds
It can still fail despite good execution
questions.explanation: Industry-level headwinds can overwhelm even a well-run individual business.

questions.question: What do low barriers to entry mean for an industry?
options: Constant new competition can be expected
Prices are always higher
The industry is shrinking

questions.explanation: Easy entry means competitors can appear quickly whenever the market looks attractive.

questions.question: Why check for regulatory requirements early?
options: To avoid needing a business model
To avoid committing capital before understanding legal obligations
Because all industries are equally regulated

questions.explanation: Discovering a costly regulatory requirement after investing is far more damaging than checking first.

lessons.title: 4.7 Competitor Analysis
lessons.html:
📖 Competitor Analysis
Understanding who else is solving this problem, and how.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Competitor Analysis

Competitor Analysis is the focus of this Market Research lesson. It helps the learner make a practical startup decision, complete an action, and support that action with evidence.

primary research

New information collected directly from people through interviews, surveys, observation, or experiments.

secondary research

Existing information gathered from reports, databases, publications, and credible online sources.

target market

The defined group of customers a business chooses to serve.

Competitor analysis maps everyone already serving your target customer's need, including informal and indirect alternatives, not just obvious direct competitors. As established earlier, whatever the customer does today is competition, even if it is a workaround rather than a company.

The purpose is not to copy the strongest competitor, but to find where they are weak or absent. A crowded market with satisfied customers is a hard place to enter; a market with common complaints about existing options is an opening.

Key points

  • List direct, indirect and informal competitors, including doing nothing.
  • For each, note price, quality, strengths and specific weaknesses customers mention.
  • Read reviews and complaints; they reveal exactly where competitors fall short.
  • Identify what you could do differently, not just what you could do the same but slightly better.
  • Reassess regularly; competitors change and new ones enter.

Example

A founder studying laundry services in her area finds three competitors, all with common complaints about slow turnaround. Rather than competing on price, she builds the business around a guaranteed same-day service, directly answering the shared complaint rather than undercutting an already-thin margin.

Why this matters

Competitor analysis done well points to an opening rather than a battle. Founders who skip it either enter a market blind to what has already failed there, or copy an incumbent closely enough to compete purely on price.

lessons.title: 📝 Practice: Competitor Analysis
lessons.html: Quick check: Review the notes and complete the two action steps, then answer these to confirm you understood Competitor Analysis.

questions.question: What counts as a competitor in this analysis?
options: Only businesses in the same city
Only companies with an identical product
Direct, indirect and informal alternatives, including doing nothing
Only businesses larger than yours
questions.explanation: Any existing way the customer meets the need today is part of the competitive picture.

questions.question: What is the purpose of reading competitor reviews and complaints?
options: To calculate their revenue
To report them to regulators
To copy their marketing language
To find specific weaknesses that represent an opening
questions.explanation: Complaints reveal exactly where an existing offer falls short of what customers want.

questions.question: What should competitor analysis lead to?
options: Identifying where competitors are weak or absent
Avoiding the market entirely
Matching every competitor's price
Copying the strongest competitor exactly
questions.explanation: The value is in finding an opening, not in imitating what already exists.

lessons.title: 4.8 SWOT Analysis
lessons.html:
📖 SWOT Analysis
A simple framework for assessing a business honestly from four angles.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

SWOT Analysis

SWOT Analysis is the focus of this Market Research lesson. It helps the learner make a practical startup decision, complete an action, and support that action with evidence.

primary research

New information collected directly from people through interviews, surveys, observation, or experiments.

secondary research

Existing information gathered from reports, databases, publications, and credible online sources.

target market

The defined group of customers a business chooses to serve.

SWOT examines Strengths and Weaknesses, which are internal to the business, alongside Opportunities and Threats, which come from outside it. The frame is simple; the value depends entirely on being honest, particularly about weaknesses founders are tempted to minimise.

A SWOT that lists only strengths and opportunities is not analysis; it is enthusiasm. The weaknesses and threats are where the real planning work happens, because they are the risks a plan must actually address.

Key points

  • Strengths and weaknesses are about the business itself: skills, resources, reputation, cost structure.
  • Opportunities and threats are about the environment: market growth, competition, regulation, technology.
  • Be specific; 'good team' is not useful, 'founder has five years in this exact industry' is.
  • For every weakness, ask what could be done about it.
  • Revisit the SWOT as the business and its environment change.

Example

A founder's SWOT lists as a weakness that she has no experience in accounting, and as a response plans to hire a part-time bookkeeper for the first year rather than manage it herself. The honest weakness produced a concrete decision; a vague or omitted weakness would not have.

Why this matters

SWOT is simple enough to overuse carelessly, producing a list nobody acts on. Done honestly, with a response attached to each weakness and threat, it becomes a genuine planning tool rather than an exercise.

lessons.title: 📝 Practice: SWOT Analysis
lessons.html: Quick check: Review the notes and complete the two action steps, then answer these to confirm you understood SWOT Analysis.

questions.question: Which two SWOT elements are internal to the business?
options: Weaknesses and threats
Strengths and weaknesses
Opportunities and threats
Strengths and opportunities
questions.explanation: Strengths and weaknesses describe the business itself; opportunities and threats describe its environment.

questions.question: Why is honesty about weaknesses the most important part of a SWOT?
options: Weaknesses are easiest to write
Weaknesses are required by investors
They are where the real planning and risk response happens
Strengths are always obvious
questions.explanation: A SWOT that avoids weaknesses produces no useful plan for addressing real risk.

questions.question: What should follow identifying a weakness?
options: Ignoring it until it becomes a problem
Comparing it to a competitor's strength only
Removing it from the list
Considering what could be done about it
questions.explanation: An identified weakness is only useful if it leads to a response.

lessons.title: 4.9 Market Trends
lessons.html:
📖 Market Trends
Reading the direction things are moving, not just their current state.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Market Trends

Market Trends is the focus of this Market Research lesson. It helps the learner make a practical startup decision, complete an action, and support that action with evidence.

primary research

New information collected directly from people through interviews, surveys, observation, or experiments.

secondary research

Existing information gathered from reports, databases, publications, and credible online sources.

target market

The defined group of customers a business chooses to serve.

A market trend is a sustained shift in customer behaviour, technology or conditions over time, as distinct from a short-term fluctuation. Recognising a genuine trend early, and distinguishing it from a passing fad, is one of the more valuable judgement calls a founder makes.

The test is durability: does the shift rest on something that persists — falling technology cost, a demographic change, a lasting behaviour shift — or on a temporary novelty that fades once the newness wears off?

Key points

  • Look for shifts grounded in durable causes: cost, demographics, infrastructure, regulation.
  • Be sceptical of trends defined mainly by social media attention; attention fades faster than behaviour changes.
  • Ask how the trend affects your specific target customer, not the market in general.
  • A trend can be an opportunity to ride or a threat to prepare for — identify which it is for you.
  • Verify with more than one source before betting a business decision on a trend.

Example

Mobile money adoption in Liberia is a durable trend, resting on infrastructure and habit that will not reverse. A viral product fad promoted by a few influencers is not the same kind of trend, and building a business around it without a durable underlying cause is a much riskier bet.

Why this matters

Confusing a fad for a trend leads to building a business on a wave that has already passed by launch. Testing for durability before committing protects against that specific and common mistake.

lessons.title: 📝 Practice: Market Trends
lessons.html: Quick check: Review the notes and complete the two action steps, then answer these to confirm you understood Market Trends.

questions.question: What distinguishes a genuine trend from a fad?
options: A trend rests on a durable cause; a fad rests on temporary novelty
A trend lasts exactly one year
A fad is always more profitable
A trend is always technology-related
questions.explanation: Durability of the underlying cause is what separates a lasting shift from a passing one.

questions.question: Why be sceptical of trends defined by social media attention alone?
options: Social media is always inaccurate
Attention fades faster than real behaviour change
Social media cannot be measured
Trends require government confirmation
questions.explanation: Visibility on a platform does not guarantee the underlying behaviour is lasting.

questions.question: What should be checked before betting a decision on a trend?
options: That competitors have not noticed it
That it started this year
That it applies to your specific target customer, verified with more than one source
That it is mentioned in the news
questions.explanation: A trend must be confirmed and shown to actually affect your customer before it justifies a decision.

lessons.title: 4.10 Research Report
lessons.html:
📖 Research Report
Turning everything gathered into something that can guide a decision.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Research Report

Research Report is the focus of this Market Research lesson. It helps the learner make a practical startup decision, complete an action, and support that action with evidence.

primary research

New information collected directly from people through interviews, surveys, observation, or experiments.

secondary research

Existing information gathered from reports, databases, publications, and credible online sources.

target market

The defined group of customers a business chooses to serve.

A research report brings together the customer discovery, market, industry, competitor and trend research into one document that supports a specific decision: whether to proceed, what to build, who to target, and at what price.

The common failure is producing a long document that describes findings without stating what they mean for the decision at hand. A research report should end with a recommendation, not merely a summary.

Key points

  • State the decision the report supports before presenting findings.
  • Summarise the evidence for each finding, with numbers where possible.
  • Separate what was found from what you conclude it means.
  • End with a specific recommendation and what would change it.
  • Keep it short enough that it will actually be read and acted on.

Example

A research report on a proposed tutoring service states upfront that it will recommend whether to launch, presents interview and pricing evidence, and concludes that 18 of 25 interviewed parents would pay the stated price — recommending a pilot with two subjects before expanding.

Why this matters

This report is what turns the whole discovery stage into a decision rather than a folder of notes. It is also the natural first section of the business plan you are building throughout this program.

lessons.title: 📝 Practice: Research Report
lessons.html: Quick check: Review the notes and complete the two action steps, then answer these to confirm you understood Research Report.

questions.question: What should a research report end with?
options: A description of the industry only
A list of competitors
A list of every interview conducted
A specific recommendation
questions.explanation: The purpose of the research is to support a decision, and the recommendation is where that decision is stated.

questions.question: What is the common failure in research reports?
options: Describing findings without stating what they mean for the decision
Including too many interviews
Being too short
Including a recommendation
questions.explanation: A report that only summarises findings without interpreting them fails to support any decision.

questions.question: Why keep the report short?
options: Short reports are always more accurate
So it will actually be read and acted on
Because long reports are illegal
To reduce the evidence presented
questions.explanation: A report nobody reads to the end cannot inform the decision it was meant to support.

lessons.title: 5.1 Business Model Basics
lessons.html:
📖 Business Model Basics
What a business model actually is, stripped to its core.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Business Model Basics

Business Model Basics is the focus of this Business Models lesson. It helps the learner make a practical startup decision, complete an action, and support that action with evidence.

business model

The system that explains how a business creates, delivers, and captures value.

value proposition

A clear promise of the benefit a customer receives and why the offer is a better choice.

revenue stream

A specific way the business earns money from customers or partners.

A business model describes how a business creates value for customers and captures some of that value back as revenue. Two questions define it completely: what do customers get, and how does the business get paid for providing it.

The same product can sit inside very different business models. A software tool can be sold once, rented monthly, given away and monetised through advertising, or bundled free with a paid service. The product is not the model; how value moves back to the business is.

Key points

  • Separate the offer (what customers get) from the revenue mechanism (how you are paid).
  • The same value can be delivered through several different models — choose deliberately.
  • A weak business model can sink a strong product, and a strong model can rescue a mediocre one.
  • Model choice affects cash flow timing as much as total revenue.
  • Revisit the model as the business grows; what worked at ten customers may not work at ten thousand.

Example

Two founders build similar tutoring apps. One sells a one-time purchase; the other charges a small monthly subscription. The second earns less per customer initially but builds predictable recurring revenue, which is worth more to a lender or investor evaluating the business a year later.

Why this matters

Confusing the product with the business model is a common early mistake. This module works through the building blocks so that model choice becomes deliberate rather than accidental.

lessons.title: 📝 Practice: Business Model Basics
lessons.html: Quick check: Review the notes and complete the two action steps, then answer these to confirm you understood Business Model Basics.

questions.question: What two questions define a business model?
options: Who the founder is, and where the business is located
How large the market is, and how fast it grows
What customers get, and how the business is paid for it
What the product costs, and who makes it
questions.explanation: Value delivered and value captured together define the model, independent of the specific product.

questions.question: Can the same product exist under different business models?
options: Only software products allow this
Only physical products allow this
No, the product determines the model
Yes, the same product can be sold, rented, or monetised differently
questions.explanation: How revenue is captured is a separate choice from what is offered.

questions.question: Why might a business choose recurring revenue over a larger one-time sale?
options: It builds predictable revenue that is valued by lenders and investors
One-time sales are illegal
Recurring revenue requires no customers
Recurring revenue is always higher in total
questions.explanation: Predictability itself has value beyond the raw revenue total, particularly when seeking financing.

lessons.title: 5.2 Business Model Canvas
lessons.html:
📖 Business Model Canvas
A one-page map of the whole business, all in one view.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Business Model Canvas

Business Model Canvas is the focus of this Business Models lesson. It helps the learner make a practical startup decision, complete an action, and support that action with evidence.

business model

The system that explains how a business creates, delivers, and captures value.

value proposition

A clear promise of the benefit a customer receives and why the offer is a better choice.

revenue stream

A specific way the business earns money from customers or partners.

The Business Model Canvas is a single-page framework with nine blocks covering every essential part of a business: customer segments, value proposition, channels, customer relationships, revenue streams, key resources, key activities, key partners and cost structure.

Its value is forcing the whole model onto one page, where the connections between blocks become visible. A canvas showing an expensive key resource with no matching revenue stream to pay for it reveals a gap that a lengthy business plan can hide in separate sections.

Key points

  • Fill in what you know; leave gaps visible rather than inventing answers.
  • Check that revenue streams actually cover the cost structure.
  • Update the canvas as you learn; it is a working document, not a final report.
  • Use sticky notes or a simple grid; the format matters less than the honesty of the content.
  • A canvas with contradictions between blocks is more useful than one that looks tidy and is wrong.

Example

A founder's canvas shows a key resource of custom software with a significant ongoing cost, but the revenue stream block shows a single low one-time fee. Seeing both on one page exposes that the model cannot sustain the resource it depends on, prompting a rethink before any code is written.

Why this matters

The remaining topics in this module work through each of the nine blocks individually. The canvas is where they come back together as one coherent, checkable model.

lessons.title: 📝 Practice: Business Model Canvas
lessons.html: Quick check: Review the notes and complete the two action steps, then answer these to confirm you understood Business Model Canvas.

questions.question: How many blocks does the Business Model Canvas have?
options: Four
Nine
Five
Twelve
questions.explanation: The nine blocks together cover every essential part of how a business creates and captures value.

questions.question: What is the main value of putting the whole model on one page?
options: It is required by law
It looks more professional
Connections and gaps between blocks become visible
It replaces the need for customer research
questions.explanation: Seeing all blocks together exposes mismatches, such as costly resources with no matching revenue.

questions.question: How should the canvas be treated?
options: As a legal filing
As a marketing brochure
As a final, unchanging document
As a working document updated as you learn
questions.explanation: It is meant to evolve with the business's understanding of itself, not to be fixed at the start.

lessons.title: 5.3 Value Proposition
lessons.html:
📖 Value Proposition
Stating exactly why a customer should choose you.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Value Proposition

Value Proposition is the focus of this Business Models lesson. It helps the learner make a practical startup decision, complete an action, and support that action with evidence.

business model

The system that explains how a business creates, delivers, and captures value.

value proposition

A clear promise of the benefit a customer receives and why the offer is a better choice.

revenue stream

A specific way the business earns money from customers or partners.

A value proposition states the specific benefit a customer gets from your offer, and why it beats their current alternative. It is not a slogan; it is a testable claim about what changes for the customer.

A strong value proposition names the customer, the problem, and the specific improvement in terms the customer would recognise from their own experience — not in terms that sound impressive to the founder.

Key points

  • State it as: for [customer], who has [problem], we offer [benefit], unlike [alternative].
  • Test the wording on an actual customer; if they do not recognise the problem, rewrite it.
  • Focus on outcome, not features; customers buy the change, not the mechanism.
  • A value proposition should be falsifiable — specific enough that it could turn out to be wrong.
  • Different segments may need different value propositions for the same underlying product.

Example

A weak value proposition reads 'innovative solutions for modern businesses.' A strong one reads 'for shop owners who lose track of slow-moving stock, we turn a phone photo into a weekly stock report, unlike paper records that only get checked at year end.' The second can be tested; the first cannot.

Why this matters

This is the sentence a customer, a partner or a lender should be able to read and immediately understand what changes for them. Every marketing message in later modules traces back to getting this sentence right.

lessons.title: 📝 Practice: Value Proposition
lessons.html: Quick check: Review the notes and complete the two action steps, then answer these to confirm you understood Value Proposition.

questions.question: What makes a value proposition strong?
options: Being specific and testable about the customer, problem and benefit
Length and detail
Matching a competitor's wording
Impressive-sounding language
questions.explanation: Specificity is what allows the claim to be checked against real customer experience.

questions.question: What should a value proposition focus on?
options: The technical features of the product
The outcome or change for the customer
The founder's background
The size of the company
questions.explanation: Customers buy the change in their situation, not the mechanism that produces it.

questions.question: Why should a value proposition be falsifiable?
options: So it satisfies legal requirements
So it can be patented
So it is specific enough that it could turn out to be wrong, and therefore testable
So it sounds more confident
questions.explanation: A vague claim that can never be wrong also can never be validated as right.

lessons.title: 5.4 Customer Segments
lessons.html:
📖 Customer Segments
Grouping customers by what they actually need, not by who they are.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Customer Segments

Customer Segments is the focus of this Business Models lesson. It helps the learner make a practical startup decision, complete an action, and support that action with evidence.

business model

The system that explains how a business creates, delivers, and captures value.

value proposition

A clear promise of the benefit a customer receives and why the offer is a better choice.

revenue stream

A specific way the business earns money from customers or partners.

Customer segments divide a market into groups that need different things from the business, or need to be reached in different ways. Segmenting by need is more useful than segmenting only by demographics, because two people of the same age and location can want completely different things.

A business can serve one segment or several, but each served segment adds complexity: a different message, sometimes a different price, sometimes a different channel. Serving more segments is not automatically better.

Key points

  • Segment by need and behaviour first, demographics second.
  • Each segment should differ enough to need a different approach; otherwise it is one segment, not two.
  • Serving fewer segments well usually beats serving many segments poorly, especially early on.
  • Revisit segmentation as the business learns who actually buys and why.
  • A segment must be reachable, not just definable, to be useful.

Example

A meal-delivery business initially defines its segment as 'busy professionals.' Interviews reveal two distinct needs within that group: some want daily variety and are price-insensitive, others want a cheap fixed weekly menu. These are functionally two segments requiring different offers, not one.

Why this matters

Getting segmentation right early prevents building one offer that half-satisfies two different groups of customers, which typically satisfies neither fully.

lessons.title: 📝 Practice: Customer Segments
lessons.html: Quick check: Review the notes and complete the two action steps, then answer these to confirm you understood Customer Segments.

questions.question: What is more useful for segmentation than demographics alone?
options: Segmenting by age only
Segmenting by location only
Not segmenting at all
Segmenting by need and behaviour
questions.explanation: Need and behaviour predict what a customer wants far better than demographic categories alone.

questions.question: When should a group be treated as two separate segments?
options: When they differ enough to need a different approach
Whenever there are more than ten customers
Only when they live in different areas
Never, one segment always covers everyone
questions.explanation: Meaningfully different needs or behaviours justify treating a group as separate segments.

questions.question: What must a segment be, beyond being definable?
options: Profitable immediately
Reachable
Large
International
questions.explanation: A segment you cannot actually reach with a message or channel is not practically useful.

lessons.title: 5.5 Customer Relationships
lessons.html:
📖 Customer Relationships
Deciding how the business interacts with customers over time.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Customer Relationships

Customer Relationships is the focus of this Business Models lesson. It helps the learner make a practical startup decision, complete an action, and support that action with evidence.

business model

The system that explains how a business creates, delivers, and captures value.

value proposition

A clear promise of the benefit a customer receives and why the offer is a better choice.

revenue stream

A specific way the business earns money from customers or partners.

This block of the canvas defines the kind of relationship a business maintains with each segment: personal one-to-one service, self-service with no direct contact, automated help, or a community customers build among themselves.

The choice affects both cost and customer expectation. Personal service costs more per customer but can justify a higher price and build loyalty; self-service scales cheaply but can feel impersonal if customers expected more contact.

Key points

  • Match the relationship type to what the segment actually expects and will pay for.
  • Personal service scales poorly; plan for it only where the margin supports it.
  • Self-service needs excellent design, since there is no person to fill the gaps.
  • A mismatch between expected and delivered relationship style is a common source of complaints.
  • The relationship type can change as the business grows and standardises.

Example

A tutoring startup begins with the founder personally messaging every parent. As it grows past thirty families, this becomes unsustainable, and she introduces a simple weekly automated update alongside monthly personal check-ins — keeping the relationship parents valued while making the model scale.

Why this matters

Choosing the relationship type deliberately, rather than letting it happen by default, prevents both the founder burning out on unscalable personal service and customers feeling abandoned by relationships that are too automated for what they expected.

lessons.title: 5.6 Channels
lessons.html:
📖 Channels
How your value proposition actually reaches the customer.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Channels

Channels is the focus of this Business Models lesson. It helps the learner make a practical startup decision, complete an action, and support that action with evidence.

business model

The system that explains how a business creates, delivers, and captures value.

value proposition

A clear promise of the benefit a customer receives and why the offer is a better choice.

revenue stream

A specific way the business earns money from customers or partners.

Channels are the paths through which customers learn about, evaluate, buy and receive support for your offer. A channel can be direct (your own shop, app or sales team) or partner-owned (a retailer, a marketplace, a distributor).

Different stages of the customer relationship can use different channels: awareness might come through social media, purchase through a marketplace, and support through WhatsApp. Consistency across these matters as much as the choice of any one channel.

Key points

  • Map each stage — awareness, evaluation, purchase, delivery, support — and choose a channel for each.
  • Owned channels give more control and margin; partner channels give more reach at a cost.
  • Match the channel to where your specific target segment already spends time and trust.
  • Too many channels early on spreads a small team too thin to do any of them well.
  • Test one channel properly before adding a second.

Example

A skincare business tries to sell simultaneously through its own website, three marketplaces and door-to-door sales in the first month. None gets enough attention to work well. Focusing on the one marketplace where the target customers already shop, and doing it properly, outperforms the scattered approach.

Why this matters

Channel choice determines both how much a business can control its customer relationship and how much reach it can achieve at what cost. Choosing deliberately, and focusing early, is what makes a small team's effort actually work.

questions.explanation: Limited attention spread across many channels usually means none is executed well enough to succeed.

lessons.title: 5.7 Revenue Streams
lessons.html:
📖 Revenue Streams
The specific ways money actually flows into the business.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Revenue Streams

Revenue Streams is the focus of this Business Models lesson. It helps the learner make a practical startup decision, complete an action, and support that action with evidence.

business model

The system that explains how a business creates, delivers, and captures value.

value proposition

A clear promise of the benefit a customer receives and why the offer is a better choice.

revenue stream

A specific way the business earns money from customers or partners.

Revenue streams are the mechanisms by which a business earns money from each customer segment: one-time sale, subscription, usage fee, licensing, commission, advertising, or renting access. A business can combine several.

Choosing a mechanism affects far more than the amount earned. It shapes cash flow timing, how predictable revenue is, and how customers perceive value — a subscription implies ongoing service in a way a one-time sale does not.

Key points

  • Match the mechanism to how the customer experiences value: continuous use suits subscription, one-off need suits a single sale.
  • Recurring revenue is generally more valuable to the business than an equivalent one-time sale, because it is predictable.
  • Usage-based pricing aligns cost with value for the customer, which can lower the barrier to starting.
  • Combining streams, such as a base fee plus usage charges, can suit some businesses better than one mechanism alone.
  • Test pricing and mechanism together; the same product can succeed or fail depending on how it is charged for.

Example

A software tool for shop inventory could be sold as a one-time purchase, a monthly subscription, or a small fee per transaction recorded. The subscription matches how the tool is actually used — continuously — and builds predictable revenue the one-time sale would not.

Why this matters

Revenue stream choice is one of the highest-leverage decisions in the whole business model, because it determines both how much is earned and how sustainable that earning is over time.

questions.explanation: Predictability of future income is valuable in itself, separate from the total amount earned.

questions.explanation: Charging in proportion to use matches what a customer pays to what they actually get.

lessons.title: 5.8 Cost Structure
lessons.html:
📖 Cost Structure
Knowing what running the business actually costs, and why the type of cost matters.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Cost Structure

Cost Structure is the focus of this Business Models lesson. It helps the learner make a practical startup decision, complete an action, and support that action with evidence.

business model

The system that explains how a business creates, delivers, and captures value.

value proposition

A clear promise of the benefit a customer receives and why the offer is a better choice.

revenue stream

A specific way the business earns money from customers or partners.

Cost structure covers everything the business spends to operate: fixed costs that do not change with volume (rent, salaries) and variable costs that scale with activity (materials, transaction fees, delivery per order).

The mix matters as much as the total. A business with high fixed and low variable costs needs volume to break even but earns strongly once it does; one with low fixed and high variable costs breaks even easily but each unit contributes less.

Key points

  • Separate fixed from variable costs explicitly; they behave very differently as the business grows.
  • High fixed costs create risk at low volume but reward at scale.
  • Low variable cost per unit means growth adds profit quickly once fixed costs are covered.
  • Know your true cost per unit before setting a price; pricing below true cost is common and dangerous.
  • Revisit cost structure as the business grows; economies of scale can change it.

Example

A bakery renting a large kitchen has high fixed costs and needs a minimum volume of orders to cover rent each month. A baker working from home has almost no fixed cost but a higher cost per item once ingredients and a smaller-scale process are accounted for. Neither structure is wrong, but they demand very different volumes to succeed.

Why this matters

Cost structure connects directly to the pricing and break-even work in Module 9. Understanding the mix of fixed and variable costs now is what makes that later financial work meaningful rather than abstract.

lessons.title: 5.9 Key Resources
lessons.html:
📖 Key Resources
What the business must have to actually deliver its value proposition.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Key Resources

Key Resources is the focus of this Business Models lesson. It helps the learner make a practical startup decision, complete an action, and support that action with evidence.

business model

The system that explains how a business creates, delivers, and captures value.

value proposition

A clear promise of the benefit a customer receives and why the offer is a better choice.

revenue stream

A specific way the business earns money from customers or partners.

Key resources are the assets a business needs to operate: physical (equipment, premises), intellectual (a recipe, a brand, software), human (specific skills), or financial (capital, credit).

The question to ask of each is not merely whether you have it, but whether it is truly necessary for this specific value proposition, or whether it is being acquired out of habit or ambition rather than need.

Key points

  • List only the resources genuinely required to deliver the current value proposition.
  • Distinguish resources you must own from those you can rent, borrow or access through a partner.
  • Human skill is a resource; be honest about gaps and how they will be filled.
  • Avoid acquiring expensive resources before the model is proven at small scale.
  • Revisit as the business grows; resources needed at scale differ from those needed to start.

Example

A founder plans to buy a delivery van before her food business has a single confirmed order. The actual key resource she needs at this stage is a reliable relationship with a motorbike courier, rented per delivery, not owned capital equipment she cannot yet justify.

Why this matters

Correctly identifying key resources prevents both under-resourcing, which limits what can be delivered, and over-resourcing, which ties up capital in assets a small, unproven business does not yet need.

lessons.html: Quick check: Review the notes and complete the two action steps, then answer these to confirm you understood Key Resources.

options: The competitors in a market

Expensive resources are always inferior
Resources cannot be resold

questions.explanation: Committing capital to assets before validating the model increases risk without corresponding evidence of return.

lessons.title: 5.10 Key Activities
lessons.html:
📖 Key Activities
What the business must actually do, every day, to deliver its value.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Key Activities

Key Activities is the focus of this Business Models lesson. It helps the learner make a practical startup decision, complete an action, and support that action with evidence.

business model

The system that explains how a business creates, delivers, and captures value.

value proposition

A clear promise of the benefit a customer receives and why the offer is a better choice.

revenue stream

A specific way the business earns money from customers or partners.

Key activities are the most important things a business must do well to make its model work: production, problem-solving, or maintaining a platform, depending on the type of business. They are not everything a business does, but the few things it cannot afford to do poorly.

Identifying them clarifies where the founder's attention and the team's effort should concentrate, as distinct from tasks that are necessary but not decisive to success.

Key points

  • Name the two or three activities that most determine whether the business succeeds.
  • Distinguish key activities from routine tasks that matter less if done imperfectly.
  • Resource and staff the key activities first; everything else can be simpler or outsourced.
  • If a key activity is being neglected in favour of easier tasks, that is a warning sign.
  • Key activities can shift as the business model shifts.

Example

For a tutoring business, the key activity is not managing a website; it is the quality of the actual teaching sessions. A founder who spends her best hours perfecting the website while tutoring quality drifts has misidentified where her attention should go.

Why this matters

This distinction between what matters most and what merely needs doing is what allows a small team to prioritise correctly under real time constraints, rather than spreading effort evenly across tasks of very different importance.

lessons.title: 📝 Practice: Key Activities
lessons.html: Quick check: Review the notes and complete the two action steps, then answer these to confirm you understood Key Activities.

options: Everything a business does

questions.question: What is a warning sign regarding key activities?
options: Reviewing them monthly

questions.explanation: What matters most to the model's success can shift as the model itself evolves.

lessons.title: 5.11 Key Partners
lessons.html:
📖 Key Partners
Who else the business depends on, and what that dependency requires.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Key Partners

Key Partners is the focus of this Business Models lesson. It helps the learner make a practical startup decision, complete an action, and support that action with evidence.

business model

The system that explains how a business creates, delivers, and captures value.

value proposition

A clear promise of the benefit a customer receives and why the offer is a better choice.

revenue stream

A specific way the business earns money from customers or partners.

Key partners are the suppliers, distributors or allied organisations a business relies on to operate. Partnerships can reduce risk, provide resources the business cannot build itself, and extend reach, but they also create dependency.

A useful partnership benefits both sides clearly enough that it survives disagreement. A partnership that only benefits one side tends to collapse under the first real strain.

Key points

  • Identify what you genuinely cannot do alone, and seek a partner for exactly that.
  • Ensure the partnership benefits both sides in ways each can articulate.
  • Put terms in writing, even with people you trust; memory of an informal deal fades and diverges.
  • Assess what happens if a key partner fails or withdraws; avoid single points of failure where possible.
  • Revisit partnerships as the business grows; a supplier suited to small volume may not suit larger volume.

Example

An entrepreneur partners with a single supplier for a key ingredient with no written agreement. When the supplier raises prices sharply during a shortage, the business has no recourse and no alternative source lined up, and margins collapse overnight.

Why this matters

Key partnerships are a form of resource the business does not have to build itself, but every dependency carries risk that must be assessed and, where possible, mitigated, not simply hoped away.

lessons.title: 📝 Practice: Key Partners
lessons.html: Quick check: Review the notes and complete the two action steps, then answer these to confirm you understood Key Partners.

options: It benefits both sides clearly enough to survive disagreement

options: Their marketing budget

questions.explanation: Understanding the consequence of losing a partner reveals how much risk that dependency carries.

lessons.title: 5.12 Business Model Review
lessons.html:
📖 Business Model Review
Testing the whole canvas for internal consistency before committing.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Business Model Review

Business Model Review is the focus of this Business Models lesson. It helps the learner make a practical startup decision, complete an action, and support that action with evidence.

business model

The system that explains how a business creates, delivers, and captures value.

value proposition

A clear promise of the benefit a customer receives and why the offer is a better choice.

revenue stream

A specific way the business earns money from customers or partners.

With all nine blocks drafted, this topic is about reviewing them together for consistency: does the cost structure match the key resources and activities; do the revenue streams actually cover the costs; does the value proposition match what the target segment said they wanted.

This review is where founders most often discover that pieces built independently do not actually fit together — a common and valuable discovery to make on paper rather than after spending money.

Key points

  • Check that revenue streams cover the full cost structure, with margin.
  • Check that key resources and activities are only what the value proposition actually requires.
  • Check that the value proposition matches evidence from real customer interviews, not assumption.
  • Look for one block that quietly contradicts another; that is usually where the real risk sits.
  • Treat this as an ongoing habit, not a one-time exercise before Module 6.

Example

A completed canvas shows a value proposition promising same-day delivery, but the key resources list only one part-time rider. The mismatch is invisible reading either block alone, and obvious the moment they are checked against each other.

Why this matters

This review is the discipline that turns nine separate answers into one coherent, testable model, and it is exactly the kind of check that is cheap to do now and expensive to discover later, after money has been spent building the mismatched pieces.

options: Writing a new value proposition

questions.explanation: Consistency across blocks is what turns nine separate answers into one coherent model.

questions.question: Where do founders most often discover a problem during this review?
options: Where one block quietly contradicts another
In the length of the document
In the font used

questions.explanation: Blocks built independently often do not actually support each other, and the contradiction is the real risk.

questions.question: How often should this kind of review happen?
options: Only once, before Module 6
As an ongoing habit as the model evolves
Only after the business fails
Only if investors request it
questions.explanation: The model continues to change as the business learns, so consistency needs checking repeatedly, not once.

lessons.title: 6.1 Product Design
lessons.html:
📖 Product Design
Designing around the customer's problem, not the founder's preference.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Product Design

Product Design is the focus of this Product Development lesson. It helps the learner make a practical startup decision, complete an action, and support that action with evidence.

minimum viable product

The simplest usable version of a solution that can test an important assumption with customers.

prototype

An early representation of a product or service used to explore, communicate, and test an idea.

customer feedback

Information from users about their experience, needs, problems, and desired improvements.

Product design is the process of deciding what a product does, how it works, and how it feels to use, in service of the problem it is meant to solve. Good design starts from the customer's need established during validation, not from what the founder finds interesting to build.

A recurring failure is designing for capability rather than for the customer: adding a feature because it is technically possible, not because a real customer asked for it or would notice its absence.

Key points

  • Trace every design decision back to a specific customer need identified earlier.
  • Favour doing one thing well over doing many things adequately, especially early on.
  • Design for the customer's actual context: their device, their connectivity, their time pressure.
  • Resist adding features that impress the founder but were not requested by real customers.
  • Revisit the design against feedback, not just against the original plan.

Example

A founder designing a farm record app is tempted to add detailed analytics dashboards. Interviews showed farmers wanted only a fast way to log a sale by voice while their hands were busy. Building the dashboard first, before the voice logging, would solve a problem nobody raised.

Why this matters

Design decisions made without reference to validated need are the most common source of wasted development effort. Anchoring every choice to something a real customer said protects against that waste.

lessons.title: 6.2 Service Design
lessons.html:
📖 Service Design
Designing the experience around a service, not only the moment of delivery.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Service Design

Service Design is the focus of this Product Development lesson. It helps the learner make a practical startup decision, complete an action, and support that action with evidence.

minimum viable product

The simplest usable version of a solution that can test an important assumption with customers.

prototype

An early representation of a product or service used to explore, communicate, and test an idea.

customer feedback

Information from users about their experience, needs, problems, and desired improvements.

Service design covers everything a customer experiences around a service, not just the core delivery moment: how they discover it, book it, wait for it, receive it, and get help afterward. Each of these touchpoints shapes whether the service feels good, independent of the core service quality.

A technically excellent service can still feel poor if booking is confusing or follow-up support is absent. Mapping the full journey reveals gaps that are invisible if attention stays only on the central service moment.

Key points

  • Map every touchpoint from first awareness to after-service support.
  • Identify the moments most likely to cause frustration, and design those carefully.
  • Consistency across touchpoints matters as much as excellence at any single one.
  • Test the full journey yourself as a customer would experience it, not just the core delivery.
  • Small friction at booking or follow-up can undo excellent core service quality.

Example

A cleaning service delivers excellent cleaning but requires customers to call during business hours to book, with no confirmation message and no way to reschedule easily. Customers rate the experience poorly despite praising the cleaning itself, because the surrounding service design was neglected.

Why this matters

Service quality is judged on the whole journey, not the core moment alone. Designing the touchpoints around the service deliberately is what turns good delivery into a good overall experience customers return for.

options: Only the core moment of service delivery

questions.explanation: The full journey, not just the central delivery moment, shapes the customer's overall experience.

options: Because it was not advertised enough
Because customers are never satisfied
Because surrounding touchpoints like booking or support may be neglected

options: Only the price list

questions.explanation: Walking through the entire experience reveals friction that reviewing the core service alone would miss.

lessons.title: 6.3 Minimum Viable Product (MVP)
lessons.html:
📖 Minimum Viable Product (MVP)
Building the smallest thing that tests the real question.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Minimum Viable Product (MVP)

Minimum Viable Product (MVP) is the focus of this Product Development lesson. It helps the learner make a practical startup decision, complete an action, and support that action with evidence.

minimum viable product

The simplest usable version of a solution that can test an important assumption with customers.

prototype

An early representation of a product or service used to explore, communicate, and test an idea.

customer feedback

Information from users about their experience, needs, problems, and desired improvements.

A minimum viable product is the smallest version of a product that lets you test a specific assumption with real customers. It is not a lesser version of the final product; it is a deliberately incomplete tool built to answer one question as cheaply as possible.

The discipline is choosing what to leave out. An MVP that tries to include every planned feature is not minimal, and defeats the purpose of testing quickly and cheaply before full investment.

Key points

  • Identify the single riskiest assumption first, and design the MVP to test exactly that.
  • Leave out anything not required to test that specific assumption.
  • An MVP can be manual behind the scenes, even if it looks automated to the customer.
  • Define in advance what result would validate or invalidate the assumption.
  • Expect to discard or heavily revise the MVP once it has answered its question.

Example

To test whether people would pay for a curated grocery delivery box, a founder manually assembles and delivers ten boxes herself for two weeks, using a simple messaging app to take orders, rather than building an app and a warehouse first. The MVP tests demand, not operational scale.

Why this matters

Building an MVP correctly is often harder than building a fuller product, because it demands discipline about what to exclude. That discipline is what keeps early-stage risk and cost proportionate to what is actually known.

options: The final product's full feature list

questions.explanation: A clear question and a defined test result are what make an MVP purposeful rather than arbitrary.

questions.explanation: What matters is testing the assumption, not whether the mechanism behind it is automated.

lessons.title: 6.4 Product Testing
lessons.html:
📖 Product Testing
Finding out whether the product actually works, before customers do.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Product Testing

Product Testing is the focus of this Product Development lesson. It helps the learner make a practical startup decision, complete an action, and support that action with evidence.

minimum viable product

The simplest usable version of a solution that can test an important assumption with customers.

prototype

An early representation of a product or service used to explore, communicate, and test an idea.

customer feedback

Information from users about their experience, needs, problems, and desired improvements.

Product testing checks whether a product functions as intended and meets the need it was designed for, before it reaches customers at scale. It includes both functional testing (does it work correctly) and usability testing (can a real person use it without confusion).

Testing with people similar to your actual target customer is essential; a founder who understands the product deeply will use it differently from someone encountering it for the first time, and will miss the confusion a new user experiences.

Key points

  • Test functionality and usability separately; a product can work correctly and still be unusable.
  • Use testers who resemble real customers, not colleagues who already understand the product.
  • Watch people use it rather than only asking whether they liked it.
  • Test the edge cases, not only the smooth expected path.
  • Fix what testing reveals before, not after, wider launch.

Example

A founder tests her app only with fellow developers, who navigate it easily. When real customers try it, half cannot find the main feature because it is hidden behind an icon developers recognised instinctively but ordinary users did not.

Why this matters

Testing with people who resemble the actual target customer, and watching their real behaviour rather than relying on their politeness, is what catches problems before they become public failures at launch.

lessons.title: 6.5 Gathering Customer Feedback
lessons.html:
📖 Gathering Customer Feedback
Collecting feedback that actually changes what you build.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Gathering Customer Feedback

Gathering Customer Feedback is the focus of this Product Development lesson. It helps the learner make a practical startup decision, complete an action, and support that action with evidence.

minimum viable product

The simplest usable version of a solution that can test an important assumption with customers.

prototype

An early representation of a product or service used to explore, communicate, and test an idea.

customer feedback

Information from users about their experience, needs, problems, and desired improvements.

Gathering feedback means systematically collecting what customers experience after using the product, in a form specific enough to act on. Vague feedback such as 'it's good' or 'needs work' cannot direct any particular change.

The most useful feedback is tied to a specific moment: what were you trying to do, what happened, what did you expect instead. General satisfaction ratings are easier to collect but much harder to act on.

Key points

  • Ask about specific recent moments, not general impressions.
  • Collect feedback close to the moment of use, while detail is still fresh.
  • Distinguish feedback about the product from feedback about price or channel; each points to a different fix.
  • Look for patterns across several customers rather than acting on one loud complaint.
  • Close the loop: tell customers when their feedback led to a change.

Example

Instead of asking 'how did you like the app,' a founder asks 'what were you trying to do the last time you opened it, and did it work?' The second question produces specific, actionable detail; the first produces a number with no direction attached.

Why this matters

Feedback collection is only valuable if it changes decisions. Specific, moment-anchored feedback, gathered consistently and reviewed for patterns, is what actually improves a product over successive versions.

questions.explanation: A single voice may not represent the wider customer base; patterns across several are stronger evidence.

lessons.title: 6.6 Product Improvements
lessons.html:
📖 Product Improvements
Turning feedback and testing into an actual, prioritised change process.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Product Improvements

Product Improvements is the focus of this Product Development lesson. It helps the learner make a practical startup decision, complete an action, and support that action with evidence.

minimum viable product

The simplest usable version of a solution that can test an important assumption with customers.

prototype

An early representation of a product or service used to explore, communicate, and test an idea.

customer feedback

Information from users about their experience, needs, problems, and desired improvements.

Product improvement is the ongoing cycle of using feedback and testing results to change the product, prioritising which changes matter most given limited time and resources. Not every piece of feedback deserves an immediate change; some changes matter far more than others.

A useful filter weighs how many customers are affected, how serious the issue is, and how cheaply it can be fixed. A minor complaint from one customer competes for the same limited development time as a serious problem affecting many, and prioritisation should reflect that difference.

Key points

  • Prioritise by combining how many are affected, how serious the issue is, and the cost to fix.
  • Fix problems that block customers from getting value before adding new features.
  • Batch small improvements; ship them together rather than constantly interrupting stability.
  • Track whether a shipped improvement actually resolved the issue it targeted.
  • Resist scope creep, where minor requests quietly expand into a much larger rebuild.

Example

Feedback reveals two issues: a rare crash affecting three power users, and a confusing checkout step causing many customers to abandon a purchase. Despite the crash sounding more dramatic, the checkout fix affects far more revenue and should be prioritised first.

Why this matters

Prioritisation, not effort alone, determines whether limited development time is spent on what actually matters most to customers and the business. This discipline is what keeps a small team's improvements proportionate to their real impact.

questions.explanation: Small requests can accumulate into major, unplanned work if not managed deliberately.

lessons.title: 6.7 Quality Control
lessons.html:
📖 Quality Control
Making sure every unit or instance of your product meets the same standard.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Quality Control

Quality Control is the focus of this Product Development lesson. It helps the learner make a practical startup decision, complete an action, and support that action with evidence.

minimum viable product

The simplest usable version of a solution that can test an important assumption with customers.

prototype

An early representation of a product or service used to explore, communicate, and test an idea.

customer feedback

Information from users about their experience, needs, problems, and desired improvements.

Quality control is the set of checks that ensure what customers actually receive matches what was promised, consistently, unit after unit or session after session. Without it, quality drifts as volume grows or as different staff deliver the service.

The check should happen as early as possible in the process, since catching a defect before it reaches a customer is far cheaper than resolving a complaint afterward, in both cost and reputation.

Key points

  • Define the standard explicitly, in terms specific enough to check against.
  • Check at the earliest point a defect could be caught, not only at the final step.
  • Keep records of what fails checks and why, to find recurring causes.
  • Train everyone delivering the product or service to the same standard.
  • Revisit standards as volume grows; what worked at ten units may not hold at a thousand.

Example

A bakery selling ten cakes a week checks each one personally before it leaves. At two hundred cakes a week with three staff baking, the same informal check is no longer possible, and a written standard with a simple checklist becomes necessary to keep quality consistent across different hands.

Why this matters

Quality drifts quietly as a business grows past what one founder can personally inspect. Building explicit checks in before that drift becomes visible to customers protects the reputation the business has already built.

questions.explanation: Volume and multiple staff outpace what one person's informal oversight can cover.

lessons.title: 6.8 Product Launch Planning
lessons.html:
📖 Product Launch Planning
Preparing everything needed before customers arrive, not after.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Product Launch Planning

Product Launch Planning is the focus of this Product Development lesson. It helps the learner make a practical startup decision, complete an action, and support that action with evidence.

minimum viable product

The simplest usable version of a solution that can test an important assumption with customers.

prototype

An early representation of a product or service used to explore, communicate, and test an idea.

customer feedback

Information from users about their experience, needs, problems, and desired improvements.

Launch planning coordinates everything that must be ready before a product goes to market: the product itself, the ability to deliver at the expected volume, the marketing message, and the plan for handling problems that surface once real customers arrive.

A common failure is treating launch as only a marketing event. A brilliant launch campaign that drives demand the operation cannot fulfil damages the business more than a quiet launch that can be served well.

Key points

  • Confirm operational capacity matches expected demand before driving traffic to it.
  • Prepare a plan for handling problems publicly and responsively once real customers arrive.
  • Decide whether to launch broadly or to a small group first, to catch issues at manageable scale.
  • Align the marketing message with what the product can actually deliver on day one.
  • Plan the days immediately after launch as carefully as launch day itself.

Example

A meal-kit business runs an enthusiastic social media launch that generates far more orders than its single kitchen can prepare. Late deliveries and complaints follow, damaging a reputation with customers this same marketing worked hard to attract. A soft launch to a smaller list would have matched demand to capacity.

Why this matters

Launch is the moment a business's operational, product and marketing readiness are all tested simultaneously. Planning it as a coordinated whole, rather than as a marketing event alone, is what protects the reputation built up to that point.

It avoids the need for a marketing message

questions.explanation: Testing at smaller scale limits the damage of any problems the full launch would otherwise expose broadly.

lessons.title: 7.1 Branding Fundamentals
lessons.html:
📖 Branding Fundamentals
What a brand actually is, beneath the logo and colours.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Branding Fundamentals

Branding Fundamentals is the focus of this Branding & Marketing lesson. It helps the learner make a practical startup decision, complete an action, and support that action with evidence.

brand

The expectations, memories, and impressions people associate with a business or offer.

positioning

The place a business wants its offer to occupy in the mind of a target customer compared with alternatives.

customer acquisition

The process and cost of attracting a prospect and converting that person into a paying customer.

A brand is the set of associations a customer has with a business: what it stands for, what they can expect, and how it makes them feel. The visual elements — name, logo, colours — express the brand, but they are not the brand itself.

A brand is built by consistent experience over time, not declared by a mission statement. What a business actually does, repeatedly, teaches customers what to expect far more than what it claims about itself.

Key points

  • A brand is what customers experience and remember, not what a business states about itself.
  • Consistency across every interaction builds a brand faster than any single impressive moment.
  • A brand promise that is broken repeatedly becomes a liability rather than an asset.
  • Small businesses build brand through direct experience before they can afford broad advertising.
  • Visual identity should express something true about the business, not disguise a weak experience.

Example

A tailor known for finishing every order exactly on the promised date builds a reputation for reliability through nothing but consistent behaviour, long before he has a logo or a slogan. That reliability is his brand, and it came from repetition, not design.

Why this matters

Understanding brand as accumulated experience, rather than as visual design alone, is what keeps the branding work in this module grounded in something real the business must actually deliver, not just present.

questions.explanation: Repeated, reliable experience shapes expectations more than any isolated impressive event.

questions.explanation: Repeated failure to deliver on what customers expect erodes rather than builds the brand.

lessons.title: 7.2 Choosing a Business Name
lessons.html:
📖 Choosing a Business Name
A practical decision, not just a creative one.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Choosing a Business Name

Choosing a Business Name is the focus of this Branding & Marketing lesson. It helps the learner make a practical startup decision, complete an action, and support that action with evidence.

brand

The expectations, memories, and impressions people associate with a business or offer.

positioning

The place a business wants its offer to occupy in the mind of a target customer compared with alternatives.

customer acquisition

The process and cost of attracting a prospect and converting that person into a paying customer.

A business name should be easy to say, spell and remember, distinct enough to search for online, and free of associations that would embarrass or confuse in your market. Creativity matters less than these practical constraints.

Checking availability matters as much as the name itself: a name already registered, trademarked, or attached to an existing domain and social handles creates problems that are expensive to fix after the business has built recognition around it.

Key points

  • Say it aloud to several people and see if they can spell it back correctly.
  • Check domain and social handle availability before falling in love with a name.
  • Check for existing businesses or trademarks using the same or a very similar name.
  • Avoid names that only make sense in one language if you may expand beyond it.
  • A slightly plain, clear name usually outperforms a clever, confusing one.

Example

A founder chooses a name that sounds appealing to her but that most people mishear and misspell when trying to find her business online. Switching to a simpler, phonetically obvious name measurably increases how often customers find her through search.

Why this matters

A name is infrastructure a business will use in every conversation, every search result, and every piece of paperwork for years. The practical checks in this topic prevent a costly rename after the business has already built some recognition.

lessons.html: Quick check: Review the notes and complete the two action steps, then answer these to confirm you understood Choosing a Business Name.

lessons.title: 7.3 Logo Design
lessons.html:
📖 Logo Design
A visual mark that works everywhere it needs to appear.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Logo Design

Logo Design is the focus of this Branding & Marketing lesson. It helps the learner make a practical startup decision, complete an action, and support that action with evidence.

brand

The expectations, memories, and impressions people associate with a business or offer.

positioning

The place a business wants its offer to occupy in the mind of a target customer compared with alternatives.

customer acquisition

The process and cost of attracting a prospect and converting that person into a paying customer.

A logo is a simple visual mark that identifies a business at a glance. Its job is recognition and legibility across many contexts — a phone screen, a receipt, a sign, a social media icon — not artistic complexity.

A logo that looks impressive as a large, detailed image often fails at small sizes, where most people will actually encounter it. Simplicity that survives shrinking matters more than intricate detail.

Key points

  • Test the logo at the smallest size it will realistically appear, such as a phone icon.
  • Ensure it works in a single colour, since colour printing or display is not always available.
  • Avoid trends that will look dated quickly; aim for something that ages reasonably.
  • A logo does not need to explain the business; the name and experience do that over time.
  • Consistency in how it is used matters as much as the design itself.

Example

A detailed, illustrative logo looks striking on a large banner but becomes an unreadable smudge as a small app icon or a social media profile picture, which is where customers most often actually see it. A simplified version built for small sizes solves this from the start.

Why this matters

A logo is judged by how well it performs at the smallest and most common sizes it appears at, not by how it looks in a single large presentation. Designing with that constraint in mind from the beginning avoids a costly redesign later.
